docs.title: Setup and notation
docs.text:
We consider binary classification with a label \(Y\in\{0,1\}\), where \(1\) is the positive class (e.g. a fraudulent transaction) and \(0\) the negative class. A model produces a real-valued score \(S=s(X)\), higher meaning “more likely positive”. A threshold \(t\) turns the score into a decision

\[\hat Y_t \;=\; \mathbf 1\{S>t\}.\]

Let \(P\) and \(N\) be the numbers of positive and negative cases and \(n=P+N\). Two quantities describe how imbalanced the data are:

\[\pi \;=\; \frac{P}{n}\quad\text{(prevalence)}, \qquad k \;=\; \frac{N}{P} \;=\; \frac{1-\pi}{\pi}\quad\text{(class ratio: negatives per positive)}.\]

For a fraud rate of \(0.1\%\) we have \(\pi=0.001\) and \(k=999\). Finally, \(S^{+}\) and \(S^{-}\) denote the score of a randomly drawn positive and negative case respectively; their distributions are the class-conditional score distributions.

docs.title: The confusion matrix
docs.text:
Fixing a threshold \(t\), every case falls into exactly one cell:

Predicted positive Predicted negative Actual positive (\(P\) cases) TP (true positive) FN (false negative) Actual negative (\(N\) cases) FP (false positive) TN (true negative)

so that \(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}=P\) and \(\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{TN}=N\). Everything below is a function of these four counts.

docs.title: Rates conditioned on the true class
docs.text:
The first four metrics divide by a row total of the confusion matrix. Each is therefore a conditional probability given the true class, which is why none of them depends on \(\pi\).

True positive rate (TPR)

Also known as recall, sensitivity, hit rate, detection rate, or power (\(=1-\) Type II error rate). It is the probability or proportion of actual positive cases that are correctly flagged as positive.

\[\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\;=\; \mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}\;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{P} \;=\; \mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=1) \;=\; \mathbb{P}(S^{+}>t).\]

False negative rate (FNR)

Also known as the miss rate or Type II error rate. It is the proportion of actual positive cases that are missed.

\[\mathop{\mathrm{FNR}}\;=\; \frac{\mathrm{FN}}{\mathrm{FN}+\mathrm{TP}} \;=\; 1-\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\;=\; \mathbb{P}(S^{+}\le t).\]

False positive rate (FPR)

The false positive rate (FPR)—also known as fall-out, false alarm rate, or Type I error rate—is the probability or proportion of actual negative cases that are incorrectly flagged as positive.

\[\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\;=\; \frac{\mathrm{FP}}{\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{TN}} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{FP}}{N} \;=\; \mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=0) \;=\; \mathbb{P}(S^{-}>t).\]

True negative rate (TNR)

Also known as specificity or selectivity. It is the proportion of actual negative cases correctly left unflagged.

\[\mathop{\mathrm{TNR}}\;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP}} \;=\; 1-\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\;=\; \mathbb{P}(S^{-}\le t).\]

docs.title: Rates conditioned on the prediction
docs.text:
The next three metrics divide by a column total: they answer “given that the model said positive (negative), how often is it right?”. They mix the two classes in the proportion \(P:N\), so they do depend on \(\pi\).

Precision (positive predictive value, PPV)

The proportion of flagged cases that are truly positive. Its complement is the false discovery rate, \(\mathrm{FDR}=1-\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\): the share of alerts that are false alarms.

\[\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}} \;=\; \mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid \hat Y_t=1).\]

Negative predictive value (NPV)

The proportion of unflagged cases that are truly negative.

\[\mathrm{NPV} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FN}} \;=\; \mathbb{P}(Y=0\mid \hat Y_t=0).\]

docs.title: Single-number summaries at one threshold
docs.text:
Accuracy and balanced accuracy

\[\mathrm{Acc} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN}}{n} \;=\; \pi\,\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+ (1-\pi)\,\mathop{\mathrm{TNR}}, \qquad \mathrm{BalAcc} \;=\; \tfrac12(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+\mathop{\mathrm{TNR}}).\]

Accuracy weights the two classes by their frequency, so under heavy imbalance it is dominated by the majority class (the accuracy paradox: with \(\pi=0.001\), a model that never flags anything has \(\mathrm{Acc}=99.9\%\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}=0\)). Balanced accuracy removes the dependence on \(\pi\) by weighting both classes equally.

\(F_1\) and \(F_\beta\) scores

\(F_1\) is the harmonic mean of precision and recall at a single threshold:

\[F_{1}\;=\; \frac{2\,\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\cdot\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}}{\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}+\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}} \;=\; \frac{2\,\mathrm{TP}}{2\,\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}}.\]

The harmonic mean punishes imbalance between the two: \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}=1\) with \(\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}=0.01\) gives \(F_{1}\approx0.02\), not \(0.5\). The general form \(F_\beta=\dfrac{(1+\beta^2)\,\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\cdot\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}}{\beta^2\,\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}+\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}}\) treats recall as \(\beta\) times as important as precision, so \(\beta>1\) favours recall. Like precision, \(F_\beta\) ignores true negatives.

Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)

The correlation between prediction and truth, using all four cells:

\[\mathrm{MCC} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}\cdot\mathrm{TN}-\mathrm{FP}\cdot\mathrm{FN}} {\sqrt{(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN})(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP})(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FN})}}\in[-1,1].\]

docs.title: The bridge identity: how \(\pi\) enters
docs.text:
The two families above are linked by the class ratio \(k=N/P\). This is the single most important identity in these notes.

Proposition 1: Prevalence enters through \(k\)

For every threshold \(t\),

\[\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\;=\; \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}}{\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+ k\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}}, \qquad F_{1}\;=\; \frac{2\,\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}}{1+\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+k\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}}, \qquad \mathrm{Acc} \;=\; \pi\,\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+(1-\pi)(1-\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}).\] Proof

Proof. By definition \(\mathrm{TP}=P\cdot\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\) and \(\mathrm{FP}=N\cdot\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\). Hence

\[\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}=\frac{P\,\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}}{P\,\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+N\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}}=\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}}{\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+k\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}}.\]

For \(F_1\), note \(2\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN} = 2P\,\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+N\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}+P(1-\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}})=P(1+\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+k\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}})\), so \(F_{1}= 2P\,\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}/\big(P(1+\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+k\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}})\big)\). The accuracy formula was shown above. ◻

Read this identity slowly: \(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\) are properties of the classifier alone (they are conditional on the class), while \(k\) is a property of the dataset. Whenever \(k\) is large, even a tiny \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\) is multiplied by a huge number inside the denominator of precision.

Metric Conditions on Uses TN? Depends on \(\pi\)? TPR (recall), FNR true class no no FPR, TNR true class yes no Precision, FDR prediction no yes NPV prediction yes yes Accuracy both yes yes Balanced accuracy true class yes no \(F_1\), \(F_\beta\) both no yes Which metrics depend on the class balance.

docs.title: Threshold-free summaries: ROC-AUC and AUC-PR
docs.text: All the metrics so far describe one threshold \(t\). As \(t\) sweeps from \(+\infty\) down to \(-\infty\), the classifier flags more and more cases and \((\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}},\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}})\) moves from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\). Tracing this path under two different choices of axes gives the two curves.

docs.title: The ROC curve and ROC-AUC
docs.text:
Definition 2: ROC curve

The receiver operating characteristic curve is the set of points \(\big(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}(t),\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}(t)\big)\) over all thresholds \(t\).

A random classifier traces the diagonal \(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}=\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\); a perfect one passes through the corner \((0,1)\). The curve is unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of the scores, since only the ranking matters.

Definition 3: ROC-AUC

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}\;=\; \int_0^1 \mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\; d\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}.\]

Theorem 4: Probabilistic interpretation

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}\;=\; \mathbb{P}(S^{+}>S^{-}) + \tfrac12\,\mathbb{P}(S^{+}=S^{-}),\]

the probability that a randomly chosen positive case is scored above a randomly chosen negative case.

Proof

Proof. Assume continuous scores with density \(f^{-}\) for negatives (ties then have probability zero). Since \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}(t)=\mathbb{P}(S^{-}>t)\), we have \(d\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}=-f^{-}(t)\,dt\), and as \(t\) runs from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\) the FPR runs from \(0\) to \(1\). Therefore

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(S^{+}>t)\,f^{-}(t)\,dt=\mathbb{P}(S^{+}>S^{-}).\]

Ties contribute half by the usual trapezoid convention. ◻

So \(\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}=0.5\) means random ranking and \(1\) means every positive is ranked above every negative. Note what does not appear in this definition: the proportion of positives.

docs.title: The precision–recall curve and AUC-PR
docs.text:
Definition 5: PR curve

The precision–recall curve is the set of points \(\big(\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}(t),\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}(t)\big)=\big(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}(t),\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}(t)\big)\) over all thresholds \(t\).

A classifier with no skill (scores independent of the label) has \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}=\pi\) at every recall level, so the PR curve’s baseline is the horizontal line at the prevalence, not at \(0.5\). True negatives never appear on either axis.

Definition 6: AUC-PR / average precision

Sort cases by decreasing score and let \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}_j,\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}_j\) be the precision and recall after the \(j\)-th distinct threshold (with \(\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}_0=0\)). The average precision is

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}\;=\; \sum_{j}\big(\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}_j-\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}_{j-1}\big)\,\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}_j \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{continuous limit}\;}\; \int_0^1 \mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\; d\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}.\]

Equivalently, \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}\) is the mean, over the \(P\) positive cases, of the precision measured at the rank of that positive.

Remark

Remark 1. “Average precision” is a recall-weighted average (weights \(\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}_j-\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}_{j-1}\)), not a plain average over thresholds. “AUC-PR” is used loosely: computing the area with the trapezoid rule instead of this step sum linearly interpolates between operating points, which is generally over-optimistic, and some benchmarks use an “interpolated” variant. Always state which one you report. The step-wise \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}\) is what sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score computes.

Figure 1 already contains the whole story: one classifier, one ROC curve, but a family of PR curves indexed by \(\pi\). Sections 3 and 4 make this precise.

docs.title: A ten-transaction toy example
docs.text:
Rank ten transactions by model score from highest to lowest. Three are fraud (P), seven are legitimate (N), and the true labels in rank order are

\[\text{P, N, P, N, N, P, N, N, N, N}.\]

Flagging the top \(j\) cases gives the operating points in Table 1.

\(j\) label TP FP TPR (recall) FPR Precision 1 P 1 0 \(1/3\) \(0\) \(1\) 2 N 1 1 \(1/3\) \(1/7\) \(1/2\) 3 P 2 1 \(2/3\) \(1/7\) \(2/3\) 4 N 2 2 \(2/3\) \(2/7\) \(1/2\) 5 N 2 3 \(2/3\) \(3/7\) \(2/5\) 6 P 3 3 \(1\) \(3/7\) \(1/2\) 7 N 3 4 \(1\) \(4/7\) \(3/7\) 8 N 3 5 \(1\) \(5/7\) \(3/8\) 9 N 3 6 \(1\) \(6/7\) \(1/3\) 10 N 3 7 \(1\) \(1\) \(3/10\)

Operating points when flagging the top \(j\) cases (\(P=3\), \(N=7\)).

ROC-AUC (pairwise view). By Theorem 4, count for each fraud how many legitimate cases it outranks: the first fraud beats all \(7\), the second beats \(6\), the third beats \(4\). Hence

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}=\frac{7+6+4}{3\times7}=\frac{17}{21}\approx0.81 .\]

AUC-PR (precision at each fraud). The precisions at the ranks of the three frauds are \(1\), \(2/3\) and \(1/2\) (the rows with label P in the table), so

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}=\frac{1+\tfrac23+\tfrac12}{3}=\frac{13}{18}\approx0.72, \qquad\text{against a baseline of } \pi=0.30.\]

Both views are drawn in Figure 2. Here \(\pi=0.3\) is not extreme, so the two metrics tell a broadly similar story. The next two examples show what happens when it is.

docs.title: One classifier, increasing imbalance
docs.text:
Take the Gaussian score model of Figure 1: negatives score \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) and positives \(\mathcal N(\mu,1)\) with \(\mu=2\). Then \(\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}=\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2)\approx0.921\). Keep the classifier exactly fixed and change only the prevalence \(\pi\), equivalently the number of legitimate cases the model has to sift through.

Prevalence \(\pi\) \(k=N/P\) ROC-AUC AUC-PR (AP) Baseline (\(=\pi\)) AP / \(\pi\) 0.5 1 0.921 0.922 0.5 1.8 0.1 9 0.921 0.665 0.1 6.7 0.01 99 0.921 0.269 0.01 26.9 0.001 999 0.921 0.062 0.001 61.8

The same classifier at four prevalences (Gaussian model, \(\mu=2\); values by numerical integration of \(\int \mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\,d\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}\)).

Proposition 7: Negative inflation, a thought experiment

Replace every negative case by \(m\) copies drawn from the same distribution (so \(N\to mN\) and \(k\to mk\)). Then for every threshold \(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}(t)\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}(t)\) are unchanged, so the ROC curve and ROC-AUC are exactly unchanged, while \(\mathrm{FP}\to m\,\mathrm{FP}\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\to\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}/(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}+mk\,\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}})\), so the PR curve and \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}\) change.

Proof

Proof. \(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\) conditions on positives, which were not touched; \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}=\mathbb{P}(S^{-}>t)\) is a probability under the (unchanged) negative score distribution. Precision follows from Proposition 1 with \(k\) replaced by \(mk\). ◻

Going from \(\pi=0.1\) to \(\pi=0.01\) in Table 2 is exactly this experiment with \(m=11\): the ROC-AUC does not move (\(0.921\)) while AP drops from \(0.665\) to \(0.269\).

Remark

Remark 2. These are population values. With a finite sample the estimate is noisy, especially when there are few positives: a simulation with \(10^6\) negatives and about \(1000\) positives gave \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}\approx0.057\) against the population value \(0.062\), whereas the ROC-AUC estimate (\(\approx0.92\)) is stable. Report confidence intervals (e.g. by bootstrap) when \(P\) is small.

docs.title: Two models that ROC-AUC cannot tell apart
docs.text:
Now compare two different classifiers on a data set of \(10^6\) transactions with \(1000\) frauds (\(\pi=0.001\), \(k=999\)). Model A catches \(60\%\) of the frauds while flagging only \(0.1\%\) of legitimate transactions; Model B catches \(80\%\) but flags \(20\%\) of legitimate transactions. Interpolating linearly to the corner \((1,1)\) gives the ROC curves in Figure 4(a).

Model TPR FPR TP FP Precision Alerts A 0.60 0.001 600 999 0.375 1 599 B 0.80 0.20 800 199 800 0.004 200 600

An investigation team would obviously prefer A. B finds a third more fraud but buries it under two hundred times as many false alarms. ROC-AUC ranks B (marginally) first; AP ranks A first by a factor of \(64\). The analytic reason is the subject of the next section.

docs.title: What each metric is trying to accomplish
docs.text:
ROC-AUC AUC-PR (AP) Question it answers “If I draw a random fraud and a random legitimate case, how often is the fraud scored higher?” “As I demand to catch more of the frauds, what fraction of my alerts are real?” Axes \(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\) vs. \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\) Precision vs. recall Uses true negatives Yes (through \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\)) No Random baseline \(0.5\) \(\pi\) (prevalence) Depends on \(\pi\) No (Theorem 4) Yes (through \(k\); Section 4) Cost of a false positive Scaled by \(1/N\): ignores how many negatives there are Scaled by \(k\): each false positive hurts more when negatives dominate Where it looks All FPR levels equally The high-precision, low-FPR region Best used when Comparing rankers, or when the class ratio is unknown or will shift Positives are rare and alerts are costly (fraud, screening, retrieval)

Heuristic summary

ROC-AUC measures ranking quality in a world where both classes are equally represented; it is a property of the two score distributions. AUC-PR measures usefulness of the alert list in the world you will actually deploy in: it bakes the class ratio into precision. When positives are rare, that second question is the one that determines whether the model is useful, and Proposition 7 shows the first question cannot even see the difference.

docs.title: Why AUC-PR is preferred under imbalance: a proof
Setting
docs.text:
Parametrise the ROC curve by recall. Assume (for simplicity) that the ROC curve is the graph of a continuous, nondecreasing function

\[g:[0,1]\to[0,1],\qquad g(r)=\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\text{ at the threshold where } \mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}=r,\qquad g(0)=0,\; g(1)=1 .\]

(In general replace \(g\) by a generalised inverse; the formulas hold as Stieltjes integrals.) Let \(r^{*}=\sup\{r:g(r)=0\}\) be the fraction of positives the model can capture before its first false alarm (\(r^{*}=0\) for most real models). The data are described by the pair \((g,k)\): \(g\) is a property of the classifier, \(k\) of the dataset.

Lemma 8: Both areas in terms of \(g\)

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}\;=\; 1-\int_0^1 g(r)\,dr, \qquad\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{AP}}(k) \;=\; \int_0^1 \frac{r}{\,r+k\,g(r)\,}\,dr .\] Proof

Proof. The unit square is split by the ROC curve into the area under it, which is \(\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}\), and the area to its left, which is \(\int_0^1 g(r)\,dr\) (integrating FPR against recall). The two add up to \(1\). The AP formula is \(\int \mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\,d\mathop{\mathrm{Rec}}\) with \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}=r/(r+k\,g(r))\) from Proposition 1. ◻

Lemma 8 is the whole argument in one line: \(k\) appears in AP and nowhere in ROC-AUC.

docs.title: ROC-AUC is blind to imbalance; AP is not
docs.text:
Theorem 9: Behaviour of AP in \(k\)

For a fixed classifier (fixed \(g\)):

  1. Monotonicity. \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}(k)\) is nonincreasing in \(k\), and strictly decreasing whenever \(g\) is not identically \(0\). Indeed \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial k}\frac{r}{r+k\,g(r)}=-\frac{r\,g(r)}{(r+k\,g(r))^{2}}\le0 .\)

  2. Baseline. For a no-skill classifier, \(g(r)=r\), so \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}=\int_0^1\frac{dr}{1+k}=\frac1{1+k}=\pi\).

  3. Collapse. \(\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}(k)=r^{*}\). In particular \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}\to0\) whenever the model cannot reach positive recall with zero false positives.

  4. ROC-AUC is constant. \(\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}\) does not depend on \(k\) (Lemma 8).

Proof

Proof. (a) is the derivative computation, integrated over \(r\). (b) is direct substitution. For (c), the integrand \(r/(r+k\,g(r))\) is bounded by \(1\) and, as \(k\to\infty\), converges pointwise to \(1\) on \((0,r^{*})\) where \(g=0\), and to \(0\) on \((r^{*},1]\) where \(g>0\) and \(r>0\). By dominated convergence \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}(k)\to r^{*}\). (d) is Lemma 8. ◻

So the same classifier has ROC-AUC fixed and AP sliding from near \(1\) (balanced) down to \(r^{*}\), which is usually \(0\), as the data become more imbalanced, exactly as in Table 2. AP is therefore sensitive to the quantity (the class ratio) that determines the real-world cost of false alarms, while ROC-AUC is not.

docs.title: The two metrics look at different parts of the ROC curve
docs.text:
Theorem 9 shows AP varies with \(k\) but does not yet explain why that is the right behaviour, nor how ROC-AUC could rank two models wrongly. The next result localises where each metric gets its value.

Theorem 10: Complementary regions

Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).

  1. ROC-AUC barely sees low FPR. The part of ROC-AUC contributed by \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le\alpha\) is \(\int_{0}^{\alpha}\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\,d\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le\alpha\).

  2. High precision lives at low FPR. If \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\ge p\) at recall \(r\), then \(g(r)\le \dfrac{(1-p)\,r}{p\,k}\le\dfrac{1-p}{p\,k}\). In particular \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}\ge\tfrac12\) forces \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le 1/k\).

  3. AP barely sees high FPR. The part of AP contributed by recall levels with \(g(r)\ge\alpha\) is at most \(\dfrac{1}{1+k\alpha}\).

Proof

Proof. (i) \(\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\le1\), so \(\int_0^\alpha \mathop{\mathrm{TPR}}\,d\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le\int_0^\alpha d\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}=\alpha\).

\(ii\) \(\mathop{\mathrm{Prec}}=r/(r+k\,g)\ge p\) rearranges to \(g\le r(1-p)/(pk)\), and \(r\le1\).

\(iii\) If \(g(r)\ge\alpha\) then \(\dfrac{r}{r+k\,g(r)}\le\dfrac{r}{r+k\alpha}\le\dfrac{1}{1+k\alpha}\), because \(r\mapsto r/(r+c)\) is increasing and \(r\le1\). The set of such \(r\) has measure at most \(1\). ◻

Corollary 11: Disjoint supports under imbalance

Let \(c>0\) and \(\alpha=c/k\). Then

\[\underbrace{\text{ROC-AUC mass from } \mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le c/k}_{\le\; c/k} \qquad\text{while}\qquad \underbrace{\text{AP mass from } \mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\ge c/k}_{\le\; 1/(1+c)} .\]

For \(\pi=0.001\) (\(k=999\)) and \(c=9\): the region \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le0.9\%\) contributes at most \(0.9\%\) of the area to ROC-AUC, yet it carries all but at most \(0.1\) of the value of AP.

In words: when \(k\) is large, ROC-AUC is decided almost entirely by the part of the curve at \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}>c/k\), where precision is already poor, and AP is decided almost entirely by the part at \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le c/k\), which ROC-AUC essentially ignores. Only the second region is operationally affordable, since an alert budget of \(B\) false alarms means \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\approx B/N=B/(kP)\).

docs.title: Ranking reversal: ROC-AUC can pick the wrong model
docs.text:
Return to Models A and B of Section 3.3, with ROC curves through \((\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}},\mathop{\mathrm{TPR}})=(a,\rho)\) and linear interpolation to \((1,1)\) (\(a=0.001,\rho=0.6\) for A; \(a=0.2,\rho=0.8\) for B), and \(k=999\).

ROC-AUC. By the trapezoid rule, \(\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}=\tfrac12 a\rho+\tfrac12(1-a)(1+\rho)\):

\[\mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}_A=0.0003+0.7992=0.7995,\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{AUC\text{-}ROC}}_B=0.08+0.72=0.8000 .\]

AP. On the first segment \(g(r)=ar/\rho\), so the integrand is the constant \(1/(1+ka/\rho)\) and the segment contributes

$\(\rho\cdot\frac{1}{1+ka/\rho}=\frac{\rho^{2}}{\rho+ka}:\qquad A:\ \frac{0.36}{0.6+0.999}=0.2251,\qquad B:\ \frac{0.64}{0.8+199.8}=0.0032 .\)$

The second segment (from \(\rho\) to \(1\)) adds \(0.0017\) for A and \(0.0004\) for B by numerical integration, so

$\(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}_A\approx0.227,\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{AP}}_B\approx0.0035,\qquad \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}_A}{\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}_B}\approx64 .\)$

Why this is not a coincidence. Model A’s entire advantage over B lies in \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\in[0,0.001]\). By Theorem 10(i) that slice can contribute at most \(0.001\) to ROC-AUC (it contributes \(0.0003\)), so B’s lead of about \(0.0008\) over the rest of the curve is enough to outweigh it. But by Theorem 10(ii) this slice is where precision can be as high as \(\tfrac12\) or more, and B has nothing there: its precision is \(0.004\) at every point of its first segment and lower beyond it, so \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}_B<0.004\) however well it ranks in the high-FPR region. Any pair of models whose ROC curves differ mainly at very low FPR can be reversed in the same way.

docs.title: Caveats and practical guidance
docs.text:
• Same information, different weighting. Davis and Goadrich showed that, on a fixed data set, one classifier’s ROC curve dominates another’s if and only if its PR curve does [@davis2006]. The two metrics differ because they integrate different regions with different weights, not because one has information the other lacks.

  • ROC-AUC is not useless. It is a valid, prevalence-free measure of ranking quality. It is the right tool when you want a property of the score distributions alone, or when the deployment class ratio is unknown or will shift. If you want to stay in ROC space under imbalance, use the partial AUC restricted to \(\mathop{\mathrm{FPR}}\le\alpha\).

  • AP is not comparable across data sets with different \(\pi\). Its baseline is \(\pi\), so always report it with the baseline, or as lift \(\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}/\pi\), or as the normalised \((\mathop{\mathrm{AP}}-\pi)/(1-\pi)\).

  • Pick the model by AP, the operating point by cost. Use AUC-PR to choose between models, then choose the threshold from precision, recall and \(F_{1}\) (or \(F_\beta\), or recall at a fixed alert budget) at the volume of alerts the investigation team can handle.

  • Mind the sample size. AP estimated from few positives is noisy; use bootstrap intervals.

For an empirical treatment of the same point see Saito and Rehmsmeier [@saito2015]; for a general introduction to ROC analysis see Fawcett [@fawcett2006].

The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets. PLOS ONE, 10(3):e0118432, 2015. T. Fawcett. An introduction to ROC analysis. Pattern Recognition Letters, 27(8):861–874, 2006.

docs.title: Binary classification
docs.text:
A binary classifier receives features \(x\) and predicts a label \(y\in\{0,1\}\). In fraud detection \(y=1\) means fraud and \(y=0\) means legitimate. The useful output is not a hard label but a probability

\[p(x) = \mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid x),\]

because decisions (block, review, allow) depend on a threshold that reflects the cost of each kind of error.

Example 1: Running example

A payment network processes \(1{,}000{,}000\) transactions, of which \(5{,}000\) are fraud. The base rate (prior) is \(\pi=\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=0.5\%\). A transaction with the pattern 3 a.m., large amount, new device occurs in \(3{,}000\) of the \(5{,}000\) frauds and in about \(10{,}000\) of the \(995{,}000\) legitimate cases.

Two ways of conditioning give very different answers:

\[\mathbb{P}(\text{pattern}\mid\text{fraud})=\tfrac{3000}{5000}=60\%, \qquad \mathbb{P}(\text{fraud}\mid\text{pattern})=\tfrac{3000}{13000}\approx 23.1\%.\]

The first describes how fraudsters behave; the second says how trustworthy an alert is. The gap between them is caused by the rarity of fraud, and odds are the cleanest way to see this.

docs.title: Odds
docs.text:
Definition: odds

For an event with probability \(p\), the odds are

\[\text{odds}(p)=\frac{p}{1-p},\qquad p=\frac{\text{odds}}{1+\text{odds}}.\]

Odds restate a probability as “for versus against”. If \(3\) of every \(13\) alerts are fraud, then \(p=3/13\approx 23\%\) and the odds are \(3:10=0.30\).

\(p\) odds \(p/(1-p)\) In words 0.5% 0.00503 about 1 fraud per 199 legitimate 10% 0.111 1 per 9 23% 0.30 3 per 10 50% 1 even odds 90% 9 9 per 1 Probability versus odds. For small \(p\) they are almost equal; they separate as \(p\) grows.

docs.title: Why odds?
docs.text:
1. Odds range over \([0,\infty)\) rather than \([0,1]\), which is one step closer to what a linear function can produce.

  2. Evidence multiplies odds. Bayes’ rule in odds form is

\[\underbrace{\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(Y=0\mid x)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} =\underbrace{\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)}{\mathbb{P}(Y=0)}}_{\text{prior odds}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\mathbb{P}(x\mid Y=1)}{\mathbb{P}(x\mid Y=0)}}_{\text{likelihood ratio}}.\] 
 The marginal $\mathbb{P}(x)$ appears in both posteriors and cancels.

Example 2

In Example 1 the prior odds are \(5000:995000\approx 0.005\) and the likelihood ratio is \(0.60/0.01=60\). Posterior odds \(=0.005\times 60=0.30\), i.e. \(3000:10000\), a \(23\%\) fraud probability. The pattern is \(60\) times more common among fraud, yet only \(23\%\) of cases showing it are fraud, because the prior odds are about \(1:199\).

docs.title: The logit (log-odds)
docs.text:
Definition: logit

\[\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(p)=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}.\]

Odds are never negative, but a linear score \(w^\top x+b\) can be any real number. The logarithm removes the last restriction: odds \(<1\) give a negative logit, odds \(=1\) give \(0\), odds \(>1\) give a positive logit, and \(0,\infty\) map to \(\mp\infty\). The logarithm also turns the product in Bayes’ rule into a sum:

\[\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid x)=\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}\pi+\ln\frac{\mathbb{P}(x\mid Y=1)}{\mathbb{P}(x\mid Y=0)}.\]

Each piece of evidence adds a number to a running score, which is exactly how a linear model works.

\(p\) odds \(\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(p)\) 1% 0.0101 \(-4.595\) 10% 0.111 \(-2.197\) 50% 1 \(0\) 90% 9 \(+2.197\) 99% 99 \(+4.595\) The logit is antisymmetric: \(\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(1-p)=-\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(p)\).

Example 3

The prior logit is \(\ln(1/199)=-5.29\). The pattern adds \(\ln 60=+4.09\), giving \(-1.20\): odds \(0.30\), probability \(23\%\). The score rose by \(4.09\) but stays negative because the prior was so low.

docs.title: The sigmoid
docs.text:
Definition: sigmoid

\[\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\qquad \sigma(\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(p))=p.\]

docs.title: Derivation.
docs.text:
Solve \(z=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\) for \(p\):

\[e^{z}=\frac{p}{1-p}\;\Rightarrow\; e^{z}(1-p)=p\;\Rightarrow\; p=\frac{e^{z}}{1+e^{z}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.\]

docs.title: Properties.
docs.text:
\(\sigma(z)\in(0,1)\); \(\sigma(0)=\tfrac12\); \(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\); \(\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\), with maximum slope \(0.25\) at \(z=0\); every \(+1\) on the score multiplies the odds by \(e\).

Key idea

Logit and sigmoid are the same relationship seen from two sides. A classifier works in score space, where addition and linear models are natural, and reports in probability space, where decisions and costs live.

docs.title: Logistic regression
docs.text:
Model

Logistic regression assumes the log-odds are linear in the features:

\[\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid x)=w^\top x+b \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid x)=\sigma(w^\top x+b).\]

docs.title: Reading the weights.
docs.text: Increasing \(x_j\) by one unit raises the score by \(w_j\) and multiplies the odds by \(e^{w_j}\) (the odds ratio). For \(w_j=0.7\), \(e^{0.7}=2.014\): the odds double. The bias \(b\) is the logit at \(x=0\) and carries the base rate.

docs.title: Why is the assumption reasonable?
docs.text:
If features within each class are Gaussian with different means and a shared covariance \(\Sigma\), then the quadratic terms cancel and

\[\ln\frac{\mathbb{P}(x\mid1)}{\mathbb{P}(x\mid0)}=(\mu_1-\mu_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}x+\text{const},\]

which is linear in \(x\); adding the prior logit changes only the bias. The assumption concerns the log-odds, not the data being Gaussian.

docs.title: Geometry.
docs.text: The boundary at threshold \(0.5\) is the hyperplane \(w^\top x+b=0\). A different threshold \(t\) shifts it parallel to itself to \(w^\top x+b=\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(t)\).

docs.title: Binary cross-entropy
docs.text:
For label \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p=\sigma(z)\), the model gives \(\mathbb{P}(y\mid x)=p^{y}(1-p)^{1-y}\). For independent examples, the negative log-likelihood is

\[\mathcal L=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl[y_i\ln p_i+(1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i)\bigr].\]

A confident wrong prediction is expensive: \(p=0.01\) on a fraud case costs \(-\ln 0.01=4.6\).

Gradient

Using \(\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)\),

\[\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z}=p-y,\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial w}=(p-y)\,x .\]

Consequences:

  1. No vanishing gradient. At \(p=0.01,\,y=1\) the cross-entropy gradient is \(-0.99\), whereas squared error gives about \(-0.0098\).

  2. Balance at the base rate. If the model outputs \(p=\pi=0.5\%\) for everyone, gradients on the \(5{,}000\) positives sum to \(-4{,}975\) and on the \(995{,}000\) negatives to \(+4{,}975\). They cancel, so the loss is minimised when predicted probability equals empirical frequency, which is why log loss yields calibrated probabilities.

The loss is convex in \((w,b)\).

docs.title: Focal loss.
docs.text: Focal loss multiplies each term by \((1-p_t)^{\gamma}\), with \(p_t\) the probability given to the true class. For \(\gamma=2\) and \(p_t=0.9\) cross-entropy is \(0.1054\) and focal loss \(0.00105\); at \(p_t=0.5\) they are \(0.693\) and \(0.173\). Easy examples are suppressed, at the cost of calibration.

docs.title: From two classes to \(K\): odds against a reference class
docs.text:
With \(K\) classes there is no single “other” class, so choose a reference (say class \(K\)) and compare every class with it:

\[\ln\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=k\mid x)}{\mathbb{P}(Y=K\mid x)}=z_k-z_K,\qquad k=1,\dots,K-1 .\]

Setting \(z_K=0\), the odds of class \(k\) against the reference are \(e^{z_k}\), and normalisation gives

\[\mathbb{P}(Y=K\mid x)=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j<K}e^{z_j}},\qquad \mathbb{P}(Y=k\mid x)=\mathbb{P}(Y=K\mid x)\,e^{z_k}.\]

This is multinomial logistic regression, with \(K-1\) weight vectors. The case \(K=2\) is ordinary logistic regression.

Example 4

Classes: legitimate (reference), card-not-present fraud, account takeover, with \(z_{\text{cnp}}=1\), \(z_{\text{ato}}=0\). Then \(\mathbb{P}(\text{legit})=1/(1+e+1)=0.212\), \(\mathbb{P}(\text{cnp})=0.576\), \(\mathbb{P}(\text{ato})=0.212\).

Choosing another reference changes the individual weights but not the probabilities: only score differences matter. This leads to the symmetric form.

docs.title: Softmax
docs.text:
Definition: softmax

\[\mathop{\mathrm{softmax}}(z)_k=\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{z_j}}.\]

Dividing numerator and denominator by \(e^{z_K}\) recovers the reference-class form. For \(K=2\), \(\mathop{\mathrm{softmax}}(z)_1=\sigma(z_1-z_2)\): the sigmoid is a two-class softmax.

docs.title: Properties.
docs.text: Outputs are positive and sum to \(1\); adding a constant to all scores changes nothing (subtract \(\max_k z_k\) in code to avoid overflow); the log-odds between any two classes is \(z_i-z_j\).

docs.title: Temperature.
docs.text:
Replace \(z\) by \(z/T\). For scores \((2,1,0)\):

\(T\) class 1 class 2 class 3 0.5 0.8668 0.1173 0.0159 1 0.6652 0.2447 0.0900 2 0.5065 0.3072 0.1863 As \(T\to0\) the output becomes one-hot; as \(T\to\infty\) it becomes uniform.

docs.title: Multi-class versus multi-label.
docs.text: Softmax assumes exactly one correct class. If several labels can hold at once, use an independent sigmoid per label.

docs.title: Categorical cross-entropy
docs.text:
With a one-hot label (\(1\) at the true class \(c\)) and softmax probabilities \(p\),

\[\mathcal L=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}y_k\ln p_k=-\ln p_c .\]

Binary cross-entropy is the case \(K=2\). The gradient with respect to the logits is again prediction minus truth:

\[\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z_k}=p_k-y_k,\]

and sums to zero across classes, consistent with shift invariance.

Example 5

Scores \((2,1,0)\) give \(p=(0.6652,0.2447,0.0900)\). If the true class is \(2\): \(\mathcal L=-\ln0.2447=1.408\), gradient \((0.6652,-0.7553,0.0900)\). If it is class \(1\): \(\mathcal L=-\ln0.6652=0.408\).

Squared error again suffers vanishing gradients for confident wrong predictions and is not the maximum-likelihood objective. In practice, frameworks fuse softmax and cross-entropy on raw logits (log-sum-exp trick) for stability.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
Example 6: Prior shift

A model trained when fraud was \(0.5\%\) is deployed at \(0.25\%\), assuming only the prior changed:

\[z_{\text{new}}=z_{\text{old}}+\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(\pi_{\text{new}})-\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}(\pi_{\text{old}})=z_{\text{old}}-0.696 .\]

Odds are multiplied by \(0.4987\). A score of \(23\%\) (odds \(0.30\)) becomes odds \(0.150\), i.e. \(13\%\). This is a bias shift, so ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are unchanged while precision at a fixed threshold changes. The same correction maps probabilities from a resampled training set back to the real base rate.

Example 7: Odds ratio

A weight of \(0.7\) on “new device” gives odds ratio \(e^{0.7}=2.014\). From baseline odds \(0.00503\) (0.5%) the new-device odds are \(0.01013\), about \(1.0\%\). Doubling odds roughly doubles a small probability, but from \(50\%\) it only reaches \(67\%\).

Example 8: Probabilities versus decisions

With \(p=(0.665,0.245,0.090)\) for (legitimate, CNP, ATO) the arg-max is legitimate, yet the fraud mass is \(33.5\%\). If account takeover is far costlier than a false alert, decide by expected cost, not arg-max.

docs.title: Cheat sheet and interview one-liners
docs.text:
Concept Formula Meaning Odds \(p/(1-p)\) for versus against, \([0,\infty)\) Logit \(\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\) log-odds, whole real line Sigmoid \(1/(1+e^{-z})\) score \(\to\) probability Logistic regression \(\sigma(w^\top x+b)\) log-odds linear in \(x\) Odds ratio \(e^{w_j}\) odds multiplier per unit BCE \(-[y\ln p+(1-y)\ln(1-p)]\) negative log-likelihood Gradient \(p-y\) prediction minus truth Softmax \(e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}\) \(K\)-class sigmoid Categorical CE \(-\ln p_c\) NLL of the true class Prior shift \(z+\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}\pi_{\text{new}}-\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}\pi_{\text{old}}\) bias adjustment

  • What is the logit? The log of the odds; it maps \((0,1)\) onto the real line so a linear model can predict it.

  • What does logistic regression assume? That log-odds are linear in the features, not that the data are Gaussian.

  • Why cross-entropy, not MSE? It is the maximum-likelihood loss, convex here, and its gradient \(p-y\) does not vanish when the sigmoid saturates.

  • How do you read a coefficient? \(e^{w}\) is the odds multiplier per unit, others fixed.

  • Sigmoid versus softmax? Sigmoid is softmax with two classes applied to the score difference.

  • Why is precision low for a rare class? Posterior odds \(=\) prior odds \(\times\) likelihood ratio; prior odds \(1:199\) shrink even a likelihood ratio of \(60\) to a \(23\%\) probability.

  • What changes under prior shift? The bias, by \(\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}\pi_{\text{new}}-\mathop{\mathrm{logit}}\pi_{\text{old}}\); ranking is unchanged, thresholds must be re-set.

  • Why can focal loss hurt calibration? It down-weights confident examples, so the minimiser is no longer the true probability; recalibrate (Platt or isotonic) before using scores as probabilities.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Say we have a noisy point. It is a single point with label \(y = 0\), sitting near a cluster of \(y = 1\) points in feature space. Compare what generalized cross entropy (GCE), cross entropy (CE), focal loss (FL), and mean absolute error (MAE) do to this point. How does GCE reduce its effect compared to CE?

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Let \(p = P(\text{class } 1 \mid x)\) be the model’s predicted probability for class 1. Since the label is \(y = 0\), the probability assigned to the labeled class is

\[p_y = 1 - p.\]

Assume the model is confident the point belongs to class 1:

\[p = 0.95, \qquad p_y = 0.05.\]

All gradients below are taken with respect to the logit \(z_y\) of the labeled class, using \(\frac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_y} = p_y(1-p_y)\).

docs.title: Cross entropy (CE)
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} = -\log p_y.\]

With \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} = -\log(0.05) \approx 3.00.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial z_y} = p_y - 1 = -0.95.\]

The gradient is close to its maximum magnitude. The noisy point pulls the decision boundary toward its wrong label as hard as a genuine misfit would.

docs.title: Generalized cross entropy (GCE)
docs.text:
Zhang and Sabuncu (2018) define

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GCE}} = \frac{1 - p_y^{\,q}}{q}, \qquad q \in (0, 1].\]

As \(q \to 0\) this recovers CE, and at \(q = 1\) it equals MAE.

With \(q = 0.7\) and \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GCE}} = \frac{1 - 0.05^{0.7}}{0.7} \approx \frac{1 - 0.123}{0.7} \approx 1.25.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GCE}}}{\partial z_y} = -\,p_y^{\,q}\,(1 - p_y) = -0.123 \times 0.95 \approx -0.117.\]

The GCE gradient equals the CE gradient multiplied by \(p_y^{\,q}\). This factor is the mechanism that reduces the effect of the noisy point: the more strongly the model disagrees with a label, the smaller that label’s influence on training.

docs.title: Focal loss (FL)
docs.text:
Lin et al. (2017) define

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FL}} = -(1 - p_y)^{\gamma} \log p_y.\]

With \(\gamma = 2\) and \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FL}} = (0.95)^2 \times 3.00 \approx 2.71.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FL}}}{\partial z_y} = (1 - p_y)^{\gamma}\bigl(\gamma\, p_y \log p_y + p_y - 1\bigr) \approx 0.9025 \times (-1.25) \approx -1.13.\]

The gradient is about \(1.2\times\) the CE gradient, not smaller. The modulating factor \((1 - p_y)^{\gamma} \approx 1\) when \(p_y\) is small, so focal loss leaves confidently wrong points essentially untouched.

Focal loss down-weights easy, correctly classified points (large \(p_y\)). That is useful for class imbalance, but it does nothing to suppress confidently wrong labels.

docs.title: Mean absolute error (MAE)
docs.text:
MAE is GCE with \(q = 1\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MAE}} = 1 - p_y.\]

With \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MAE}} = 0.95.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MAE}}}{\partial z_y} = -\,p_y(1 - p_y) = -0.05 \times 0.95 \approx -0.05.\]

MAE gives the smallest push from the noisy point, but it learns slowly and can underfit.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Loss Value Logit gradient Relative to CE CE 3.00 \(-0.95\) \(1\times\) Focal (\(\gamma = 2\)) 2.71 \(-1.13\) \(\approx 1.2\times\) GCE (\(q = 0.7\)) 1.25 \(-0.12\) \(\approx 0.12\times\) MAE (\(q = 1\)) 0.95 \(-0.05\) \(\approx 0.05\times\)

docs.title: How GCE reduces the effect compared to CE
docs.text:
The gradient of CE with respect to the logit is \(p_y - 1\), which does not depend on how confident the model is that the label is wrong. GCE multiplies this gradient by \(p_y^{\,q}\):

  • Confident and correct points (\(p_y \approx 0.9\)): the factor is \(0.9^{0.7} \approx 0.93\), so training is nearly unchanged from CE.

  • Confident and wrong points (\(p_y \approx 0.05\), the noisy point): the factor is \(0.05^{0.7} \approx 0.12\), so the gradient shrinks by about \(8\times\).

The noisy point still contributes a small push, but the correctly labeled \(y=1\) cluster now dominates the boundary.

docs.title: Why focal loss does not help here
docs.text:
Focal loss scales the gradient by \((1 - p_y)^{\gamma}\), which is small when the model agrees with the label. GCE scales by \(p_y^{\,q}\), which is small when the model disagrees with the label. Those are opposite cases:

  • Focal loss reduces the weight of easy examples. It helps class imbalance but not label noise.

  • GCE reduces the weight of confidently disagreeing examples. It helps label noise but can underfit hard, correctly labeled minority examples.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
