docs.title: What drift is
docs.text:
A model is trained on historical data with joint distribution \(P_{\text{train}}(X,Y)\) and then applied to new data with joint distribution \(P_{\text{serve}}(X,Y)\). Drift is the gap between the two growing over time:

\[P_{\text{train}}(X,Y)\neq P_{\text{serve}}(X,Y).\]

The result is silent degradation: the model keeps producing scores and no error is raised, but the scores become less reliable.

Two related ideas are often both called “drift”:

  • Data drift: the inputs \(X\) change.

  • Concept drift: the meaning of the inputs changes, i.e. the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) changes.

In one sentence

Drift is when production data stops matching training data, so performance decays without any error being raised.

docs.title: The three types of drift
docs.text:
The joint distribution can be factorised in two ways:

\[P(X,Y)=P(Y\mid X)\,P(X)=P(X\mid Y)\,P(Y).\]

Each type of drift corresponds to one factor changing while the others (ideally) stay fixed.

Type What changes Fraud example Main effect Covariate shift \(P(X)\) (the inputs) Festival-season volume, a new payment channel, a new user segment Model faces unfamiliar inputs and extrapolates badly Prior / label shift \(P(Y)\) (the fraud rate) An attack wave raises prevalence from \(0.1\%\) to \(0.5\%\) Probabilities are miscalibrated and the threshold is no longer optimal Concept drift \(P(Y\mid X)\) (the relationship) Fraudsters change tactics, so a pattern that used to mean fraud now looks normal The model’s learned logic is wrong; the most damaging type

Covariate shift. \(P(X)\) changes but \(P(Y\mid X)\) is unchanged. The model’s rule is still correct, but it is being applied in regions of input space where it saw little training data.

Prior (label) shift. \(P(Y)\) changes but \(P(X\mid Y)\) is unchanged. Even with a perfect, unchanged classifier, precision changes. With fixed true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR), and prevalence \(\pi=P(Y=1)\),

\[\text{Precision}=\frac{\text{TPR}\cdot\pi}{\text{TPR}\cdot\pi+\text{FPR}\cdot(1-\pi)}.\]

Example: with \(\text{TPR}=0.8\) and \(\text{FPR}=0.001\),

\[\begin{aligned} \pi=0.001:&\quad \text{Precision}=\frac{0.0008}{0.0008+0.000999}\approx 0.44,\\[2pt] \pi=0.005:&\quad \text{Precision}=\frac{0.004}{0.004+0.000995}\approx 0.80. \end{aligned}\]

The same classifier looks twice as good purely because the fraud rate changed. This is also why precision-based metrics such as AUCPR depend on prevalence.

Concept drift. \(P(Y\mid X)\) changes. The same input now has a different probability of being fraud, so the model’s learned decision boundary is simply wrong. Because input distributions can look unchanged, this type cannot be seen from the inputs alone and requires labels.

In one sentence

Covariate shift is inputs changing, prior shift is the base rate changing, and concept drift is the input-to-label relationship changing; fraud mostly suffers concept drift.

docs.title: How drift unfolds over time
docs.text:
• Sudden: an abrupt change, such as a new attack or a pipeline or schema change.

  • Gradual: the old pattern slowly gives way to a new one.

  • Incremental: a series of small steps that add up.

  • Recurring / seasonal: patterns that return, such as festivals, month-end and salary cycles.

Why it matters. Sudden drift needs fast alerts and rollback, gradual drift needs trend monitoring, and seasonal drift needs seasonality-aware baselines so that we do not retrain in a panic every year.

docs.title: Why fraud is special
docs.text:
1. Adversarial adaptation. Fraudsters probe and adapt to avoid blocks, so the drift is caused by an opponent.

  2. Feedback loop and selection bias. Blocked fraud disappears from our data, so future training data under-represents the fraud we already catch.

  3. Delayed labels. Chargebacks and investigations take weeks, so recent data looks cleaner than it really is.

  4. Non-malicious change. App releases, logging changes, upstream bugs and new products shift features without any change in fraud.

  5. Asymmetric cost. Missed fraud and false alarms both cost money, and drift can hurt each differently.

In one sentence

In fraud, drift is expected, not exceptional, because the adversary adapts and our own blocking changes the data we see.

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text:
Every drift check does the same thing. We take two samples of data:

  • the reference sample: data from the baseline period (usually the training set, or a recent stable month), containing \(n_{\text{ref}}\) rows;

  • the current sample: data from the window we are monitoring (e.g. the last day or week), containing \(n_{\text{cur}}\) rows;

and we ask how different are they? This question has two distinct parts, and different tools answer different parts.

Part 1: how big is the difference? (effect size). PSI, KL divergence, JS divergence and the KS statistic \(D\) each condense the gap between the two samples into one number.

Part 2: could the difference be just luck? (hypothesis test). Two samples drawn from exactly the same distribution never look identical, because proportions and averages wobble from sample to sample. A hypothesis test starts from

\[H_0:\ \text{both samples come from the same distribution (no drift)},\]

and computes the p-value: the probability, if \(H_0\) were true, of seeing a gap at least as large as the one observed. A small p-value means luck alone is an unlikely explanation. The KS test and the chi-square test are of this type.

Both parts are needed. With millions of rows, a test will flag gaps that are real but too small to matter; with a few hundred rows, a large and important gap may fail to reach significance. So we read the size of the difference and the evidence that it is real together.

Detection is organised in three layers, depending on what we can observe:

Layer What is compared Typical tools Needs labels? Input Distribution of each feature (and combinations of features) PSI, KS, \(\chi^2\), KL, JS, adversarial validation No Output Distribution of the model’s scores and the alert rate PSI, KS on the score No Performance Precision, recall, PR-AUC Matured cohorts, proxies, audit sample Yes

docs.title: Setup and notation
docs.text:
Pick one feature, for example the transaction amount. To compare two samples of a continuous feature, we first cut its range into \(B\) bins using edges \(b_0<b_1<\dots<b_B\).

  • The edges are computed from the reference sample only (e.g. its deciles, so each reference bin holds \(10\%\) of the rows) and then reused unchanged for the current sample. If the edges were recomputed on the current data, the bins would silently move with the data and the comparison would be meaningless.

  • For a categorical feature, the bins are simply the categories. Missing values get their own bin.

Then, for each bin \(i=1,\dots,B\):

\[e_i=\frac{\text{number of reference rows in bin } i}{n_{\text{ref}}} \quad\text{(\emph{expected} share: training-time data)},\] \[a_i=\frac{\text{number of current rows in bin } i}{n_{\text{cur}}} \quad\text{(\emph{actual} share: data now)}.\]

Both are proportions, so \(\sum_i e_i=1\) and \(\sum_i a_i=1\). If there is no drift, \(a_i\approx e_i\) for every bin. With decile bins, \(e_i=0.1\) for all \(i\), and the \(a_i\) simply tell us how the current rows are spread across the training deciles.

These two vectors, \(e=(e_1,\dots,e_B)\) and \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_B)\), are the inputs to everything below.

docs.title: Population Stability Index (PSI)
docs.text:
Definition.

\[\boxed{ \mathrm{PSI}=\sum_{i=1}^{B}(a_i-e_i)\,\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i} }\]

What each piece means. For every bin we multiply two quantities:

  • \(a_i-e_i\): the absolute shift, i.e. by how many percentage points the share of this bin moved.

  • \(\ln(a_i/e_i)\): the relative shift on a log scale. It is \(0\) if the share did not change, positive if the bin grew, negative if it shrank, and it treats doubling (\(\ln2\approx0.69\)) and halving (\(-\ln2\)) symmetrically.

Why multiply them? The absolute shift alone ignores context: moving from \(0.01\) to \(0.02\) is a doubling, whereas moving from \(0.40\) to \(0.41\) is barely a change, yet both are a shift of \(0.01\). The log-ratio alone would over-react to bins containing almost no data. The product weighs both:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{rare bin: } e=0.01,\ a=0.02:&\quad 0.01\cdot\ln 2\approx 0.00693,\\ \text{common bin: } e=0.40,\ a=0.41:&\quad 0.01\cdot\ln 1.025\approx 0.00025. \end{aligned}\]

The same absolute shift counts about \(28\) times more in the rare bin. For fraud this is desirable, since risky behaviour usually lives in sparsely populated bins.

Each term is non-negative. If \(a_i>e_i\), both factors are positive; if \(a_i<e_i\), both are negative, and their product is again positive. So shifts in different bins add up and cannot cancel each other. Consequently \(\mathrm{PSI}\ge 0\), with \(\mathrm{PSI}=0\) exactly when \(a=e\). Swapping \(a\) and \(e\) leaves the value unchanged, so PSI is symmetric.

Worked example. Reference shares \(e=(0.5,0.3,0.2)\); current shares \(a=(0.4,0.3,0.3)\).

Bin \(i\) \(e_i\) \(a_i\) \(\ln(a_i/e_i)\) \((a_i-e_i)\ln(a_i/e_i)\) 1 0.5 0.4 −0.2231 \((-0.1)(-0.2231)=0.0223\) 2 0.3 0.3 0 0 3 0.2 0.3 0.4055 \((0.1)(0.4055)=0.0406\) PSI 0.063

A larger shift, \(a=(0.2,0.3,0.5)\), gives \((-0.3)\ln0.4+0+(0.3)\ln2.5\approx0.275+0.275=0.550\).

How to read the value. The common rule of thumb is:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{PSI}<0.1&:\ \text{stable},\\ 0.1\le\mathrm{PSI}\le0.25&:\ \text{moderate shift, investigate},\\ \mathrm{PSI}>0.25&:\ \text{significant shift}. \end{aligned}\]

By this rule the first example (\(0.063\)) is stable and the second (\(0.550\)) is a significant shift. These thresholds are conventions that originated in credit scoring; they are not a hypothesis test and carry no p-value.

Noise floor. Even with no drift at all, sampling noise gives PSI a positive value. For small differences, \(\ln(a_i/e_i)\approx(a_i-e_i)/e_i\), so \(\mathrm{PSI}\approx\sum_i(a_i-e_i)^2/e_i\), and one can show that under no drift

\[\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{PSI}]\approx(B-1)\left(\frac{1}{n_{\text{ref}}}+\frac{1}{n_{\text{cur}}}\right).\]

For example, with \(B=10\) and \(n_{\text{ref}}=n_{\text{cur}}=1000\), the noise floor is \(9\times0.002=0.018\). PSI computed on small windows or with many bins is therefore noisy, and a value near this floor means nothing.

Practical caveat. If some bin has \(e_i=0\) or \(a_i=0\), the logarithm is undefined. Fix this by merging sparse bins or replacing zeros with a tiny constant (e.g. \(10^{-4}\)). A bin that is empty in the reference but populated now (a brand-new category) is itself an important drift signal.

docs.title: KL divergence
docs.text:
PSI works, but where does it come from? It is built from the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, which measures how badly one distribution describes data that actually come from another.

Definition. For two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) over the same bins (or categories),

\[\boxed{ D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\,\|\,Q)=\sum_{i}P_i\ln\frac{P_i}{Q_i} }\]

where \(P_i\) and \(Q_i\) are the probabilities of bin \(i\) under \(P\) and \(Q\). The result is in nats (natural logarithm). For drift monitoring, we take \(P=a\) (current) and \(Q=e\) (reference).

Intuition: accumulated evidence. Suppose one observation falls in bin \(i\). The quantity \(\ln(P_i/Q_i)\) is the log-likelihood ratio: how much more strongly this observation supports “the data follow \(P\)” than “the data follow \(Q\)”. If the data really follow \(P\), the bins occur with frequencies \(P_i\), so the average evidence per observation is \(\sum_iP_i\ln(P_i/Q_i)\), which is exactly the KL divergence. Hence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) is the average amount of evidence, per observation, with which we could tell the current data apart from the reference. After \(n\) observations we have accumulated about \(n\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) nats of evidence, a fact that reappears in the chi-square test below.

Properties.

  • Non-negative, zero only if identical. Using \(\ln x\le x-1\),
\[-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\sum_iP_i\ln\frac{Q_i}{P_i}\le\sum_iP_i\Big(\frac{Q_i}{P_i}-1\Big)=\sum_iQ_i-\sum_iP_i=0,\]

so \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\ge0\), with equality iff \(P=Q\).

  • Asymmetric. \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\neq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)\) in general, so it is not a distance. \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a\|e)\) weights bins by how common they are in the current data.

  • Can be infinite. If \(Q_i=0\) while \(P_i>0\) (e.g. a new device type that never appeared in the reference), the term \(\ln(P_i/0)\) is infinite. The reverse direction blows up if a reference category vanishes.

Link to PSI. Adding the two directions,

\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a\|e)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(e\|a)=\sum_ia_i\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i}+\sum_ie_i\ln\frac{e_i}{a_i}=\sum_i(a_i-e_i)\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i}=\mathrm{PSI}.\]

So PSI is the symmetrised KL divergence, which explains why it is symmetric and non-negative.

Check on the example (\(a=(0.4,0.3,0.3)\), \(e=(0.5,0.3,0.2)\)):

\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a\|e)=0.4\ln0.8+0.3\ln1.5\approx-0.0893+0.1216=0.0324,\] \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(e\|a)=0.5\ln1.25+0.2\ln\tfrac{2}{3}\approx0.1116-0.0811=0.0305,\]

and the sum \(0.0629\) matches the PSI computed above.

docs.title: Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence
docs.text:
KL has two awkward features: it is asymmetric and it can be infinite. JS divergence removes both.

Definition. Let \(M\) be the average of the two distributions, \(M_i=\tfrac12(P_i+Q_i)\). Then

\[\boxed{ \mathrm{JS}(P,Q)=\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\,\|\,M)+\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\,\|\,M) }\]

Intuition. Instead of comparing \(P\) directly with \(Q\), compare each of them with their midpoint \(M\). Whenever \(P_i>0\) or \(Q_i>0\), the midpoint satisfies \(M_i>0\), so no logarithm ever has a zero in the denominator. A category that exists only in the current data is no longer “infinitely surprising”; it simply contributes a large but finite amount.

Properties.

  • Symmetric: \(\mathrm{JS}(P,Q)=\mathrm{JS}(Q,P)\).

  • Always finite and bounded: \(0\le\mathrm{JS}\le\ln2\approx0.693\) nats (equivalently \(0\) to \(1\) bit if \(\log_2\) is used). The maximum occurs when \(P\) and \(Q\) have no overlap at all. Having a fixed scale makes the number easy to interpret: \(0\) means identical, \(\ln 2\) means completely disjoint.

  • \(\sqrt{\mathrm{JS}}\) is a true distance metric.

Worked example (\(P=a=(0.4,0.3,0.3)\), \(Q=e=(0.5,0.3,0.2)\)). The midpoint is \(M=(0.45,0.30,0.25)\):

\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|M)=0.4\ln\tfrac{0.4}{0.45}+0.3\ln\tfrac{0.3}{0.25}\approx-0.0471+0.0547=0.0076,\] \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|M)=0.5\ln\tfrac{0.5}{0.45}+0.2\ln\tfrac{0.2}{0.25}\approx0.0527-0.0446=0.0080,\] \[\mathrm{JS}=\tfrac12(0.0076+0.0080)\approx0.0078,\]

which on a scale whose maximum is \(0.693\) is a very small difference.

When to prefer which. Use PSI when you want the familiar rule-of-thumb thresholds that risk teams already know. Use JS when bins may be empty or categories can appear and disappear, or when you want a bounded score comparable across features.

docs.title: Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test (continuous features)
docs.text:
Purpose. PSI, KL and JS need binning, and the answer can depend on how the bins were chosen. The KS test compares two samples of a continuous feature directly, with no bins, and gives a p-value.

Definition. For a sample, the empirical CDF is

\[F(x)=\frac{\text{number of rows with value}\le x}{\text{number of rows}},\]

the fraction of rows at or below \(x\). Let \(F_{\text{ref}}\) and \(F_{\text{cur}}\) be the two empirical CDFs. The KS statistic is

\[\boxed{ D=\sup_x\big|F_{\text{ref}}(x)-F_{\text{cur}}(x)\big| }\]

the largest vertical gap between the two curves.

Intuition. If both samples come from the same distribution, their CDFs lie almost on top of each other. \(D\) takes values in \([0,1]\) and has a concrete reading: \(D=0.10\) means that at some value \(x^\ast\), the share of transactions below \(x^\ast\) differs by 10 percentage points between the two samples. It detects shifts in location, scale and shape, and is most sensitive near the middle of the distribution rather than the extreme tails.

Test. Under \(H_0\) (same distribution), \(D\) is of the order of \(1/\sqrt{n}\) and shrinks as the samples grow. At the \(5\%\) significance level we reject \(H_0\) when

\[D>1.358\sqrt{\frac{n_{\text{ref}}+n_{\text{cur}}}{n_{\text{ref}}\,n_{\text{cur}}}}.\]

Example of statistical versus practical significance.

  • \(n_{\text{ref}}=n_{\text{cur}}=1{,}000\): the threshold is \(1.358\sqrt{0.002}\approx0.061\), so a gap of about 6 percentage points is needed.

  • \(n_{\text{ref}}=n_{\text{cur}}=1{,}000{,}000\): the threshold is \(1.358\sqrt{2\times10^{-6}}\approx0.0019\), so a gap of just \(0.2\) percentage points is “significant”.

This is why, for large samples, \(D\) (the effect size) should be read together with the p-value. Also note that KS assumes continuous data: with many tied values (e.g. amounts rounded to whole rupees), its p-values become conservative.

docs.title: Chi-square test (categorical features)
docs.text:
Purpose. For a categorical feature (payment channel, device type, merchant category), or a binned continuous feature, we want to know whether the counts per category in the current sample are consistent with the reference proportions, or whether the gap is bigger than sampling luck explains. The chi-square (\(\chi^2\)) test answers this.

Setup. There are \(K\) categories. Under \(H_0\) (no drift), each current row falls into category \(k\) with the reference probability \(e_k\). Let

  • \(O_k\): the observed count in category \(k\) in the current sample;

  • \(E_k=n_{\text{cur}}\,e_k\): the expected count if there were no drift.

Statistic.

\[\boxed{ \chi^2=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{(O_k-E_k)^2}{E_k} }\]

Why this form?

  • \(O_k-E_k\) is the gap between what we saw and what we expected.

  • We square it so that over-counts and under-counts both add to the total rather than cancelling.

  • We divide by \(E_k\) because the natural noise in a count is about \(\sqrt{E_k}\) (counts behave roughly like a Poisson variable, whose variance equals its mean). A gap of 10 on an expected count of 20 is huge, while a gap of 10 on an expected count of 10,000 is negligible. The ratio \(z_k=(O_k-E_k)/\sqrt{E_k}\) measures the gap in units of its own noise, so each \(z_k\) is roughly a standard normal variable under \(H_0\).

Thus \(\chi^2=\sum_kz_k^2\) is a sum of squared (approximately) standard normal variables. Because the counts must add up to \(n_{\text{cur}}\), one of the \(K\) terms is determined by the others, so under \(H_0\)

\[\chi^2\sim\chi^2_{K-1}\qquad(K-1\text{ degrees of freedom}),\]

a distribution whose average value is \(K-1\).

How to read it. If there is no drift, \(\chi^2\) should be close to \(K-1\). A value far above that suggests drift. The p-value is \(P(\chi^2_{K-1}\ge\chi^2_{\text{obs}})\). For \(K=3\) (2 degrees of freedom) the \(5\%\) critical value is \(5.99\).

Worked example. Reference shares \(e=(0.5,0.3,0.2)\); current sample of \(n_{\text{cur}}=1000\) with observed counts \(O=(400,300,300)\). Expected counts: \(E=(500,300,200)\).

\[\chi^2=\frac{(400-500)^2}{500}+\frac{(300-300)^2}{300}+\frac{(300-200)^2}{200}=20+0+50=70\gg5.99,\]

so we reject \(H_0\): drift is almost certain. The same proportions with \(n_{\text{cur}}=100\) (\(O=(40,30,30)\), \(E=(50,30,20)\)) give \(\chi^2=2+0+5=7\), which only just exceeds \(5.99\).

Key caveats.

  • Size grows with sample size. For fixed proportions, \(\chi^2=n_{\text{cur}}\sum_k(a_k-e_k)^2/e_k\) grows linearly with \(n_{\text{cur}}\). The same tiny shift becomes “significant” with enough data (the example above: \(0.07\times1000=70\)). Report an effect size (PSI, or \(\sum_k(a_k-e_k)^2/e_k\)) next to the p-value.

  • Needs reasonable counts. The normal approximation requires \(E_k\gtrsim5\); rare categories should be merged.

  • Connection to KL. For small shifts, \(\chi^2\approx2\,n_{\text{cur}}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a\|e)\). In the example above, \(2\times1000\times0.0324\approx65\), close to \(70\). This is the “accumulated evidence \(\approx n\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\)” idea from the KL section, now turned into a formal test.

docs.title: Adversarial validation
docs.text:
Purpose. The tools above look at one feature at a time. Adversarial validation looks at all features together and answers: can a model tell the current data apart from the reference data?

Procedure.

  1. Label every reference row \(s=0\) and every current row \(s=1\), and stack them into one dataset.

  2. Train a classifier (e.g. gradient-boosted trees) to predict \(s\) from the features \(X\).

  3. Evaluate it with cross-validated (held-out) AUC. Without held-out evaluation, a flexible model can memorise rows and look falsely good.

Intuition. If there is no drift, the labels \(s\) are essentially coin flips as far as \(X\) is concerned, so no classifier can beat chance and AUC \(\approx0.5\). If the distributions differ, the classifier can exploit the differences, and the AUC rises towards \(1\). The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen current row receives a higher “looks-current” score than a randomly chosen reference row, so it is a direct measure of how separable the two samples are. As a rough guide, AUC below about \(0.55\) is benign, and values around \(0.7\) or above indicate substantial drift.

What it gives.

  • Where: the classifier’s feature importances (e.g. permutation importance or SHAP) show which features drive the separation.

  • Multivariate sensitivity: it detects changes in the relationships among features, which univariate tests miss.

  • A by-product: its predicted probability yields the density ratio used for importance weighting in Section 7.

Caution. Remove timestamps, row IDs and other fields that trivially identify the period, otherwise the classifier separates the samples for a meaningless reason.

docs.title: Multivariate drift
docs.text:
Checking each feature separately can miss drift entirely. Example: transaction amount and hour of day each have the same marginal distribution as before (so PSI and KS on each feature are quiet), but large amounts used to occur mostly in the daytime and now occur mostly at night. Only the joint distribution changed, and for fraud this is exactly the kind of change that matters.

Ways to catch it: adversarial validation (above); comparing correlation matrices between the two periods; or reducing the data to a few dimensions (principal components, or the model’s own internal embedding) and applying the same distance and test tools there.

docs.title: Many features, many tests
docs.text: A model with hundreds of features, checked daily, will produce false alarms by chance: at a \(5\%\) significance level, about 1 in 20 features flags even when nothing has changed. Rely on effect-size thresholds (PSI, \(D\)) and rank features by the magnitude of the shift rather than counting raw p-values below \(0.05\).

docs.title: Output layer (needs no labels)
docs.text:
What is compared. Let \(s(x)\in[0,1]\) be the model’s score for a transaction \(x\). The score is a one-number summary of all the features as the model uses them, so monitoring its distribution is a compact, label-free drift detector aligned with what the model actually does. We compare the reference and current score distributions with the same tools as above (PSI and KS on the score).

Alert rate. For a decision threshold \(\tau\), the alert (or block) rate is

\[r(\tau)=P\big(s(X)\ge\tau\big).\]

It also matters operationally, since it determines review-queue workload. It also has a useful structure. If the classifier’s TPR and FPR at \(\tau\) are unchanged and only the fraud prevalence \(\pi\) moves,

\[r=\text{TPR}\cdot\pi+\text{FPR}\cdot(1-\pi).\]

With \(\text{TPR}=0.8\) and \(\text{FPR}=0.001\), moving \(\pi\) from \(0.1\%\) to \(0.5\%\) takes the alert rate from \(0.0008+0.000999\approx0.18\%\) to \(0.004+0.000995\approx0.50\%\), nearly a threefold jump from prior shift alone.

How to read it.

  • Alert rate rises and features also drifted: likely covariate shift.

  • Alert rate rises with stable features: likely a rise in prevalence, or a change in the fraud pattern.

  • Alert rate stable does not prove the model is fine: under concept drift the model may keep flagging the same number of cases but the wrong ones.

docs.title: Performance layer (needs labels)
docs.text:
Metrics. At threshold \(\tau\),

\[\text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad\text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\]

where \(TP\), \(FP\), \(FN\) are the counts of true positives, false positives and false negatives; PR-AUC is the area under the precision–recall curve.

The problem: labels arrive late. Chargebacks and investigations take weeks, so the most recent transactions have unreliable labels. We therefore use:

  • Matured cohorts: evaluate on data old enough that its labels have settled (e.g. transactions from 60 or more days ago). This is trustworthy but always looks backwards.

  • Proxy metrics for the recent past: refund and dispute rates, customer complaints, review-queue precision (the share of flagged cases that human reviewers confirm).

  • A random audit sample: draw transactions at random, have them labelled by humans, and estimate precision and recall from them. Because it is random, it is unbiased, unlike the blocked-and-reviewed data, which is selected by the model itself. Since fraud is rare, one usually samples more heavily from high-score strata and weights each sampled case by the inverse of its sampling probability. The uncertainty of an estimated precision \(\hat p\) from \(n\) audited flagged cases is about \(\hat p\pm1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\).

Interpreting a change in performance. Precision and PR-AUC depend on the prevalence \(\pi\) (see Section 2), so a change in them does not by itself prove the classifier got worse. A rank-based metric that does not depend on \(\pi\), such as ROC-AUC or recall at a fixed false positive rate, helps separate the causes:

Observation What it points to Inputs drifted, but ROC-AUC and recall at fixed FPR are unchanged Covariate shift that has not hurt the model so far Alert rate and PR-AUC changed, but ROC-AUC and recall at fixed FPR are unchanged Prior shift (prevalence changed) ROC-AUC or recall at fixed FPR dropped Concept drift (or covariate shift severe enough to hurt) Inputs, scores and rank metrics all stable, but precision from the audit dropped Check label definition and label lag before blaming the model

Caveat. A statistically significant drift is not necessarily a performance drop. Only labels (or good proxies) tell us whether it matters.

docs.title: Summary of the tools
docs.text:
Tool Data type What it tells us Output PSI Binned or categorical Size of the shift; symmetrised KL; rule-of-thumb thresholds A number \(\ge0\) KL divergence Binned or categorical Average evidence per row that current differs from reference; asymmetric A number \(\ge0\) (can be \(\infty\)) JS divergence Binned or categorical Bounded, symmetric, always-finite version of KL A number in \([0,\ln2]\) KS test Continuous Largest gap between the two CDFs; no binning \(D\in[0,1]\) and p-value Chi-square test Categorical or binned Whether the count gaps exceed what luck explains \(\chi^2\) and p-value Adversarial validation All features jointly How separable the two samples are, and which features separate them AUC and importances

In one sentence

I monitor inputs, outputs and performance: input and score drift give early warning without labels, effect-size measures (PSI, KL, JS, \(D\)) say how big the shift is, tests (KS, \(\chi^2\)) say whether it is more than luck, and audited matured cohorts confirm whether the model really degraded.

docs.title: Diagnosing whether it is real
docs.text:
Before retraining, find the cause:

  • Pipeline or schema bug? Check for null spikes, unit changes, or a feature that became constant.

  • Seasonality? Compare with the same period last year.

  • Label lag? Recent precision may look wrong because labels have not settled.

  • Segment-specific? Slice by channel, merchant, geography and device.

  • Real adversarial change? Look for new clusters or behaviour patterns.

Retraining on a data bug simply bakes the bug into the model.

docs.title: Responding to drift
docs.text:
Short term. Recalibrate or move the threshold (the usual fix for prior shift), add or tighten rules as a stopgap, and route more cases to human review.

Prior shift correction. If the classifier was trained with prevalence \(\pi_{\text{train}}\) and is now deployed where the prevalence is \(\pi_{\text{new}}\), the posterior odds are rescaled by the ratio of prior odds:

\[\frac{p_{\text{new}}(y=1\mid x)}{p_{\text{new}}(y=0\mid x)} = \frac{p_{\text{train}}(y=1\mid x)}{p_{\text{train}}(y=0\mid x)} \cdot \frac{\pi_{\text{new}}/(1-\pi_{\text{new}})}{\pi_{\text{train}}/(1-\pi_{\text{train}})}.\]

For \(\pi\) moving from \(0.1\%\) to \(0.5\%\), the odds multiplier is

\[\frac{0.005/0.995}{0.001/0.999}\approx 5.0.\]

Covariate shift: importance weighting. Reweight training examples by the density ratio

\[w(x)=\frac{p_{\text{serve}}(x)}{p_{\text{train}}(x)}.\]

This ratio can be estimated with the adversarial classifier from Section 5. If \(\hat p(s=1\mid x)\) is its predicted probability that \(x\) comes from the serving data, then

\[w(x)\approx\frac{\hat p(s=1\mid x)}{\hat p(s=0\mid x)}\cdot\frac{n_{\text{train}}}{n_{\text{serve}}}.\]

The alternative is to retrain on data that covers the new region of input space.

Retraining. On a schedule plus triggers (drift alarm, performance drop). Choose the window carefully: recent data tracks new patterns but is noisy, whereas older data is stable but stale. Weighting recent samples is a common compromise.

Safe deployment. Shadow mode, champion/challenger comparison, staged rollout and a rollback plan.

Online or incremental learning where the problem allows it, with care for noisy or poisoned updates.

Fighting the feedback loop. Keep a small randomised exploration or holdout slice, so that we still observe what we would otherwise have blocked.

In one sentence

I diagnose first and then respond proportionally: a threshold or calibration fix for prior shift, retraining for concept drift, with shadow testing and rollback.

docs.title: Designing for drift (prevention)
docs.text:
• Prefer stable, hard-to-game signals and diverse feature families, so that no single feature can be spoofed.

  • Use time-based validation and rolling backtests to estimate how fast a model decays.

  • Version features and data, and monitor feature freshness and quality.

  • Build dashboards and alerts per feature and per segment.

  • Plan the retraining cadence from measured decay, not from a guess.

docs.title: Q1. Features look stable but precision dropped. What happened?
docs.text: Most likely concept drift: \(P(Y\mid X)\) changed, so the same inputs now mean something different. Other possibilities are prior shift (higher or lower prevalence changes precision even for an unchanged classifier), a threshold issue, label-lag artefacts, or a change in the label definition.

docs.title: Q2. How would you detect drift with delayed labels?
docs.text: Monitor inputs (PSI, KS, adversarial validation) and score distributions, track proxy metrics, run a random audit sample, and evaluate on matured cohorts.

docs.title: Q3. How often do you retrain?
docs.text: Based on measured decay and drift triggers, not a fixed guess, and always validated in shadow mode first.

docs.title: Q4. How do fraudsters affect your training data?
docs.text: Through selection bias: blocked fraud disappears from the data. Keep an exploration or holdout slice so that these cases are still observed.

docs.title: First-Step Analysis: Interview Questions and Answers
How to read the trees
docs.text:
\(E_s\) is the expected number of additional tosses from state \(s\). Each branch is one toss. A leaf shows

\[(\text{new state's expectation} + 1)\times(\text{probability of that branch}),\]

where the \(+1\) pays for the toss just made. A leaf that stops the game shows \(1\times\) probability. Adding the leaves gives the equation for the state.

docs.title: Question 0: Expected Tosses Until HH
docs.text:
Question: A fair coin is tossed until two Heads appear in a row (HH). What is the expected number of tosses?

Answer:

Reading the leaves of the tree:

\[E_1=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(E_0+1)=1+\tfrac12E_0 \quad\text{(1)}\] \[E_0=\tfrac12(E_1+1)+\tfrac12(E_0+1)=\tfrac12E_1+\tfrac12E_0+1 \quad\text{(2)}\]

Put (1) into (2):

\[E_0=\tfrac12\Bigl(1+\tfrac12E_0\Bigr)+\tfrac12E_0+1 =\tfrac32+\tfrac34E_0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tfrac14E_0=\tfrac32\] \[\boxed{E_0=6}.\]

docs.title: Question 1: Expected Tosses Until the First Head
docs.text:
Question: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until the first Head appears. What is the expected number of tosses?

Answer:

\[E=\frac12(1)+\frac12(E+1)\] \[E=1+\frac12E \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac12E=1\] \[\boxed{E=2}.\]

docs.title: Question 2: Expected Rolls Until the First 6
docs.text:
Question: A fair six-sided die is rolled until the first 6 appears. What is the expected number of rolls?

Answer:

\[E=\frac16(1)+\frac56(E+1)\] \[E=1+\frac56E \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac16E=1\] \[\boxed{E=6}.\]

docs.title: Question 3: Expected Tosses Until HHT Appears
docs.text:
Question: A fair coin is tossed until the pattern HHT first appears. Find the expected number of tosses.

States: \(E_0\) = nothing matched, \(E_1\) = last toss H, \(E_2\) = last two tosses HH.

Note that from \(E_2\) another H leaves you in \(E_2\), since the last two tosses are still HH.

Answer:

Reading the leaves:

\[E_2=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(E_2+1)\quad\Rightarrow\quad E_2=2,\] \[E_1=\tfrac12(E_2+1)+\tfrac12(E_0+1)=2+\tfrac12E_0,\] \[E_0=\tfrac12(E_1+1)+\tfrac12(E_0+1)\quad\Rightarrow\quad E_0=E_1+2.\]

Substituting \(E_1\) gives \(E_0=4+\tfrac12E_0\), so

\[\boxed{E_0=8}.\]

docs.title: Question 4: Random Walk Intuition
docs.text:
Question: What is the main idea behind first-step analysis in random-walk problems?

Answer:

A random walk moves between states. The key observation is:

After taking the next step, the process is again in a state whose future behavior can be described by the same expectation equations.

The general form, with \(E=0\) at every stopping state, is:

\[E(\text{current state}) = \sum P(\text{next state})\bigl[E(\text{next state})+1\bigr].\]

docs.title: Question 5: Gambler’s Ruin Intuition
docs.text:
Question: How does first-step analysis help in Gambler’s Ruin problems?

Answer:

Suppose a gambler currently has \(i\) dollars. If \(E_i\) denotes the expected time until ruin or victory from state \(i\), then reading the leaves,

\[E_i=p\,(E_{i+1}+1)+q\,(E_{i-1}+1)=1+pE_{i+1}+qE_{i-1}, \qquad E_0=E_N=0.\]

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
\[\boxed{ E(\text{state}) = \sum P(\text{branch})\bigl[E(\text{new state})+1\bigr] }\]

Draw the tree, write each leaf as (new expectation \(+1\)) \(\times\) probability, and add the leaves.

docs.title: MLE and MAP
docs.text:
At a glance

\[\boxed{ \hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=\arg\max_\theta \log p(D\mid\theta) \qquad \hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_\theta \big[\log p(D\mid\theta)+\log p(\theta)\big] }\]

MLE asks which parameter makes the observed data least surprising. MAP adds a log-prior, so it is the same objective plus a regularizer. A flat prior makes them identical, and as \(n\to\infty\) the prior washes out.

docs.title: Prerequisites (quick mental check)
docs.text:
• Probability basics: random variables, PDFs/PMFs, independence. The i.i.d. assumption lets the likelihood factor into a product.
  • Common distributions: Bernoulli, Binomial, Gaussian, (Poisson).
  • Logs and calculus: product \(\to\) sum, derivative set to zero.
  • Likelihood vs probability: \(p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\) viewed as a function of \(\theta\) with data fixed; not a distribution over \(\theta\).
  • Expectation and variance: needed for the bias discussion.

Optional later: KL divergence (MLE \(\equiv\) minimizing KL between the empirical distribution and the model), Fisher information (asymptotic normality, Cramér–Rao).

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) the \(n\) observed data points \(\theta\) unknown model parameter \(p(x\mid\theta)\) probability (or density) of \(x\) when the parameter is \(\theta\) \(L(\theta)\) likelihood, \(L(\theta)=p(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\theta)\), as a function of \(\theta\) \(\prod\) product, \(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i = a_1 a_2\cdots a_n\) \(\arg\max_\theta f(\theta)\) the value of \(\theta\) that maximizes \(f\) \(\hat\theta\) an estimate of \(\theta\) computed from data

i.i.d. Independent: one point tells nothing about another, so the joint factors into a product (\(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\)). Identically distributed: all points share the same distribution and the same \(\theta\).

docs.title: MLE: the core idea
docs.text:
MLE asks: which parameter value makes the data I actually saw least surprising? For i.i.d. data,

\[L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i\mid\theta),\qquad \hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=\arg\max_\theta L(\theta).\]

Key idea: likelihood vs probability

\(L(\theta)\) has the same formula as the probability of the data, but \(\theta\) varies and the data is fixed. It does not integrate to 1 over \(\theta\) and is not "the probability that \(\theta=0.7\)". That statement needs a prior (MAP/Bayes).

docs.title: Why maximize the log-likelihood
docs.text:
Since \(\log\) is strictly increasing, \(\arg\max_\theta \log L(\theta)=\arg\max_\theta L(\theta)\) (the maximizer keeps the same location in \(\theta\)). Reasons to use it:

  • Product \(\to\) sum: \(\log\prod_i p(x_i\mid\theta)=\sum_i\log p(x_i\mid\theta)\), easier to differentiate.
  • Numerical stability: a product of many numbers \(<1\) underflows to \(0\); a sum of logs does not.

Common mistake

Taking the log does not create uniqueness of the maximizer; \(L\) and \(\log L\) have identical maximizers. (Log-concavity of a model can help, but it is a separate property.)

docs.title: Recipe
docs.text:
1. Write \(L(\theta)=\prod_i p(x_i\mid\theta)\).
  2. Take the log; drop any terms without \(\theta\).
  3. Differentiate, set to \(0\), solve.
  4. Check the second derivative is negative (a max, not a min), and that the answer lies in the valid parameter range.

Sanity check

If \(\theta\) is a probability and you get \(\hat\theta=2\), there is an algebra slip. Re-check the chain rule: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\log(1-\theta)=-\frac{1}{1-\theta}\).

docs.title: MLE for the Bernoulli (coin)
docs.text:
Sequence H,H,T with \(\theta=P(\text{heads})\): \(L(\theta)=\theta^2(1-\theta)\), so \(\log L=2\log\theta+\log(1-\theta)\) and

\[\frac{2}{\theta}-\frac{1}{1-\theta}=0\;\Rightarrow\;2(1-\theta)=\theta\;\Rightarrow\;\hat\theta=\tfrac23 .\]

Second derivative \(-\frac{2}{\theta^2}-\frac{1}{(1-\theta)^2}<0\), so \(\log L\) is concave and \(2/3\) is the unique maximum.

General case: \(k\) heads in \(n\) flips.

\[\log L(\theta)=k\log\theta+(n-k)\log(1-\theta) \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{k}{\theta}=\frac{n-k}{1-\theta} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=\frac{k}{n}}\]

Where is \(\binom{n}{k}\)? If you record only the count \(k\), \(P(k\mid\theta)=\binom nk\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}\) and \(\log L=\log\binom nk+k\log\theta+(n-k)\log(1-\theta)\). The term \(\log\binom nk\) does not contain \(\theta\), so it vanishes on differentiation. This is exact (no Stirling approximation). Likewise, for a specific sequence there is no coefficient at all. General rule: any factor of \(L(\theta)\) independent of \(\theta\) can be dropped.

docs.title: MLE for the Gaussian
docs.text:
For i.i.d. \(x_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\),

\[p(x\mid\mu,\sigma^2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big),\] \[\log L(\mu,\sigma^2)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 .\]

Mean. \(\mu\) appears only in the last term, so maximizing over \(\mu\) means minimizing the sum of squared errors \(\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\). Differentiating: \(-2\sum_i(x_i-\mu)=0\), so

\[\hat\mu_{\text{MLE}}=\frac1n\sum_i x_i\quad\text{(the sample mean).}\]

It is the mean of the sample, an estimate of the unknown true \(\mu\).

Variance. With \(v=\sigma^2\) and \(\mu=\hat\mu\):

\[-\frac{n}{2v}+\frac{1}{2v^2}\sum_i(x_i-\hat\mu)^2=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}=\frac1n\sum_i(x_i-\hat\mu)^2}\]

docs.title: Bias: why the sample variance uses \(n-1\)
docs.text:
Intuition (lead with this in interviews)

You used the data to compute \(\bar x\), so the deviations are forced to satisfy \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\). Only \(n-1\) of them are free: \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. Also, \(\bar x\) minimizes \(\sum_i(x_i-c)^2\) over \(c\), so \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\le\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\), which makes dividing by \(n\) underestimate \(\sigma^2\).

Exact calculation. Using \(\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2+n(\bar x-\mu)^2\):

\[\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\Big]=n\sigma^2,\qquad \mathbb{E}\big[n(\bar x-\mu)^2\big]=n\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar x)=\sigma^2,\] \[\Rightarrow\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\Big]=(n-1)\sigma^2 .\]

Hence dividing by \(n-1\) is unbiased, while \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2\).

  • The MLE is biased but consistent: the bias \(\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\).
  • The \(n-1\) estimate is the larger of the two. For \(n=100\) the ratio is \(100/99\approx1\%\) (small); for \(n=5\) it is \(25\%\).
  • The sample standard deviation is still slightly biased (concavity of \(\sqrt{\cdot}\), Jensen).

docs.title: MLE and loss functions
docs.text:
Core principle

Minimizing a loss = maximizing a log-likelihood under some noise assumption. Loss \(=\) negative log-likelihood (NLL), purely because optimizers are conventionally written to minimize.

docs.title: Gaussian noise \(\Rightarrow\) MSE
docs.text:
For \(y_i=f(x_i;\theta)+\varepsilon_i\), \(\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\):

\[\log L(\theta)=\text{const}-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i\big(y_i-f(x_i;\theta)\big)^2,\]

so maximizing \(\log L\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) minimizing the squared error (MSE up to the factor \(1/n\)).

docs.title: Laplace noise \(\Rightarrow\) MAE
docs.text:
Density \(p(y\mid f)=\frac{1}{2b}\exp(-|y-f|/b)\):

\[\log L(\theta)=-n\log(2b)-\frac1b\sum_i|y_i-f(x_i;\theta)| ,\]

so MLE minimizes \(\sum_i|y_i-f(x_i;\theta)|\), the absolute-error (L1) loss.

docs.title: Location estimate: mean vs median
docs.text:
Noise Loss Location estimate Gaussian squared mean Laplace absolute median

Why median: nudging \(m\) right increases the distance to points on the left and decreases it to points on the right; \(\sum_i|x_i-m|\) stops improving when half the points lie on each side. Example: \(\{1,2,3,4,100\}\) has mean \(22\) but median \(3\). The Laplace density has heavier tails than the Gaussian, so a far point is less surprising and pulls the fit less (linear vs quadratic penalty): MAE is robust to outliers.

docs.title: Bernoulli \(\Rightarrow\) binary cross-entropy
docs.text:
Let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p_i=f(x_i;\theta)=P(y_i=1\mid x_i)\).

  1. One point (exponents act as a switch): \(P(y_i\mid x_i;\theta)=p_i^{\,y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\). Check: \(y_i=1\to p_i\), \(y_i=0\to1-p_i\).
  2. Dataset (independence): \(L(\theta)=\prod_i p_i^{\,y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\).
  3. Log: \(\log L=\sum_i\big[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\big]\).
  4. Negate and average (dividing by \(n\) does not change the argmin):
\[\boxed{\mathrm{BCE}(\theta)=-\frac1n\sum_i\big[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\big]}\]

With a constant \(p_i=\theta\) this reduces to the coin formula \(k\log\theta+(n-k)\log(1-\theta)\).

docs.title: Categorical \(\Rightarrow\) multi-class cross-entropy
docs.text:
Labels are one-hot \(y_{ik}\in\{0,1\}\), \(\sum_k y_{ik}=1\); the model gives \(p_{ik}=P(\text{class }k\mid x_i)\) (typically via softmax), \(\sum_k p_{ik}=1\).

\[P(y_i\mid x_i;\theta)=\prod_{k=1}^K p_{ik}^{\,y_{ik}},\quad L(\theta)=\prod_i\prod_k p_{ik}^{\,y_{ik}},\quad \log L=\sum_i\sum_k y_{ik}\log p_{ik},\] \[\boxed{\mathrm{CE}(\theta)=-\frac1n\sum_i\sum_{k=1}^K y_{ik}\log p_{ik}}\]

With one-hot labels the inner sum collapses to \(-\log p_{i,c}\) (\(c\) = true class). Binary cross-entropy is the \(K=2\) special case. Examples: assigned probability \(0.25\Rightarrow\) loss \(-\log0.25=\log4\approx1.386\); probability \(1\Rightarrow\) loss \(0\); probability \(\to0\Rightarrow\) loss \(\to\infty\) (confident wrong answers are punished very harshly).

Interview: why cross-entropy and not MSE for logistic regression?

  • BCE is exactly the NLL of a Bernoulli model, which matches a \(0/1\) label; MSE assumes Gaussian noise, which does not.
  • With a sigmoid output, the MSE gradient vanishes when the model is confidently wrong (saturation), so learning stalls. For softmax/sigmoid + CE, the gradient with respect to the logits is simply \(p-y\), which stays large exactly when the model is wrong.

docs.title: MLE summary and weakness
docs.text:
1. \(L(\theta)=p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\) as a function of \(\theta\); a product for i.i.d. data.
  2. Take the log (product \(\to\) sum, stable), maximize, drop terms without \(\theta\).
  3. Bernoulli: \(\hat\theta=k/n\). Gaussian: sample mean; \(\hat\sigma^2\) with \(1/n\) (biased, consistent).
  4. Loss = NLL: Gaussian \(\to\) MSE, Laplace \(\to\) MAE, Bernoulli \(\to\) BCE, categorical \(\to\) CE.
  5. Properties: consistent, asymptotically normal, invariant under reparametrization.

Weakness: overfitting to small data. Three flips, three heads: \(L=\theta^3\), \(\log L=3\log\theta\), derivative \(3/\theta\) has no zero. Since \(\theta\in[0,1]\), the maximum is at the boundary, \(\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=1\) (agrees with \(k/n\)). This says tails are impossible, though a fair coin gives 3 heads with probability \(1/8\). MLE trusts the data completely and cannot express prior knowledge. MAP fixes this.

docs.title: MAP: the core idea
docs.text:
Bayes' rule:

\[\underbrace{p(\theta\mid D)}_{\text{posterior}}=\frac{\overbrace{p(D\mid\theta)}^{\text{likelihood}}\;\overbrace{p(\theta)}^{\text{prior}}}{p(D)},\]

where \(p(D)\) does not depend on \(\theta\). Then

\[\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_\theta p(\theta\mid D)=\arg\max_\theta\big[\log p(D\mid\theta)+\log p(\theta)\big].\]

So MAP = MLE objective + log-prior.

  • Flat prior \(\Rightarrow\) \(\log p(\theta)\) is constant \(\Rightarrow\) MAP \(=\) MLE.
  • Framing: MLE (frequentist): \(\theta\) is a fixed unknown constant, the data is random. MAP (Bayesian): \(\theta\) is a random variable with a distribution (prior \(\to\) posterior), the data is observed.
  • MAP is only "half Bayesian": it uses a prior but reports a single point (the posterior peak) instead of the full distribution.

docs.title: MAP for the coin with a Beta prior
docs.text:
Prior: \(p(\theta)\propto\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}\), with hyperparameters \(\alpha,\beta>0\). (\(\alpha=\beta=1\) is flat; \(\alpha=\beta=2\) is a mild belief that the coin is roughly fair.)

Log-posterior (constants dropped):

\[J(\theta)=(k+\alpha-1)\log\theta+(n-k+\beta-1)\log(1-\theta).\]

Let \(A=k+\alpha-1\), \(B=n-k+\beta-1\), so \(J=A\log\theta+B\log(1-\theta)\).

\[\frac{dJ}{d\theta}=\frac A\theta-\frac B{1-\theta}=0 \;\Rightarrow\;A(1-\theta)=B\theta \;\Rightarrow\;\theta=\frac{A}{A+B},\]

and \(A+B=n+\alpha+\beta-2\). Hence

\[\boxed{\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}=\frac{k+\alpha-1}{n+\alpha+\beta-2}}\]

Second derivative \(-\frac{A}{\theta^2}-\frac{B}{(1-\theta)^2}<0\) when \(A,B>0\), so it is a maximum.

  • Check: \(\alpha=\beta=1\) gives \(k/n\) (MLE).
  • Example: \(k=n=3\), \(\alpha=\beta=2\): \(\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}=\frac{3+2-1}{3+2+2-2}=\frac45=0.8\), versus \(\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=1\).
  • Pseudo-counts: the prior acts like \((\alpha-1)\) imaginary heads and \((\beta-1)\) imaginary tails added before the real data. With \(\alpha=\beta=2\): \((3+1)/(3+2)=4/5\).
  • Washing out: as \(n\to\infty\), \(k\) and \(n\) dominate \(\alpha,\beta\), so \(\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}\to k/n=\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}\).

docs.title: Still to cover
docs.text:
1. Regularization link: Gaussian prior on weights \(\to\) L2 (ridge); Laplace prior \(\to\) L1 (lasso), derived like MSE/MAE from MLE.
  2. MAP vs MLE vs full Bayesian: when MAP helps (small data, overfitting, high dimension); limits (point estimate; not invariant under reparametrization, unlike MLE).
  3. Rapid-fire interview questions on MLE and MAP together.
  4. Open question: with \(\alpha=\beta=2\) and 30 heads in 30 flips, what is \(\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}\)? (Use the boxed formula; compare with the 3-flip case.)

docs.title: Puzzle 1: Piano Tuners in Hyderabad
docs.text:
Question: Estimate the number of piano tuners in Hyderabad.

Answer: This is a Fermi estimation problem. A reasonable approach is:

  1. Estimate the number of pianos in Hyderabad.

  2. Estimate the average number of tunings per piano per year.

  3. Estimate how many tunings a single tuner can perform annually.

  4. Compute

\[\text{Tuners} = \frac{\text{Total Tunings Per Year}}{\text{Tunings Per Tuner Per Year}}.\]

The exact number is less important than a logical decomposition and reasonable assumptions.

docs.title: Puzzle 2: Model Has 99.9% Accuracy
docs.text:
Question: A model has 99.9% accuracy on 1 million rows. Is it good?

Answer: The first question should be:

“What is the class distribution?”

If the dataset is highly imbalanced, accuracy can be misleading. For example, if 99% of observations belong to one class, a model predicting only the majority class achieves 99% accuracy while being useless.

Additional metrics to inspect:

  • Precision

  • Recall

  • F1-score

  • ROC-AUC or PR-AUC

docs.title: Puzzle 3: Recommendation Algorithms
docs.text:
Question: Algorithm A has CTR = 5.1%. Algorithm B has CTR = 5.4%. Can we conclude B is better?

Answer: No.

Things to check:

  • Sample size

  • Randomized A/B test design

  • Statistical significance

  • Confidence interval of the lift

  • Business significance

A small increase may simply be random variation.

docs.title: Puzzle 4: Expected Tosses Until First Head
docs.text:
Question: A fair coin is tossed until the first Head appears. What is the expected number of tosses?

Answer: Let the expectation be \(E\).

\[E=\frac12(1)+\frac12(1+E)\]

Solving:

\[E=2.\] \[\boxed{E=2}\]

This is an example of first-step analysis.

docs.title: Puzzle 5: Feature X Increased Sales
docs.text:
Question: A manager says:

“Sales increased after Feature X launched, therefore Feature X caused the increase.”

Answer: Correlation is not causation.

Potential confounders:

  • Seasonality

  • Marketing campaigns

  • Existing business trend

  • Competitor actions

  • Holidays or special events

A better approach is an A/B test or a causal inference framework.

docs.title: Puzzle 6: Traffic Lights in Hyderabad
docs.text:
Question: Estimate the number of traffic lights in Hyderabad.

Answer: One possible decomposition:

  1. Estimate the number of major intersections.

  2. Estimate the proportion that use traffic lights.

  3. Estimate the average number of signal units per intersection.

The focus is on assumptions and reasoning rather than the final numerical answer.

docs.title: Puzzle 7: Cancer Detection Metrics
docs.text:
Question: For a cancer detection model, which is more important: Accuracy, Precision, or Recall?

Answer: Usually Recall is most important because false negatives are very costly.

\[\text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}\]

Missing a cancer patient is often worse than generating an extra false alarm.

However, the correct metric depends on the business and medical costs associated with false positives and false negatives.

docs.title: Puzzle 8: Heavy Ball Puzzle
docs.text:
Question: One of eight balls is heavier than the others. Using a balance scale, what is the minimum number of weighings required to identify it?

Answer: Two weighings.

Reason:

Each weighing has three outcomes:

  • Left heavier

  • Right heavier

  • Equal

Two weighings provide

\[3^2=9\]

possible outcome patterns, which is enough to distinguish among eight candidate balls.

docs.title: Puzzle 9: First Look at a CSV Dataset
docs.text:
Question: You receive a CSV containing 100 columns. What is the first thing you do?

Answer: First understand the schema:

  • What is the target variable?

  • Classification or regression?

  • Data types?

  • Missing values?

  • Duplicates?

Then examine the target distribution and begin exploratory data analysis.

docs.title: SQL Roadmap for Data Science Interviews
docs.text:
14 days, one hour a day, for someone who already thinks in pandas.

Week 1 covers the basics. Week 2 covers what interviewers test most: CTEs, window functions and dates, applied to fraud-style questions.

docs.title: Setup (Day 0, 20 minutes)
docs.text:
• Dialect: learn PostgreSQL syntax, which is the safest default for interviews.

  • Where to practise: install DuckDB (pip install duckdb). It runs SQL directly on pandas DataFrames, so you can write a query and check it against the pandas version you already know.

  • Daily format: 20 minutes on the concept, then 40 minutes typing queries yourself.

docs.title: Week 1: the basics

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Say we have a noisy point. It is a single point with label \(y = 0\), sitting near a cluster of \(y = 1\) points in feature space. Compare what generalized cross entropy (GCE), cross entropy (CE), focal loss (FL), and mean absolute error (MAE) do to this point. How does GCE reduce its effect compared to CE?

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Let \(p = P(\text{class } 1 \mid x)\) be the model’s predicted probability for class 1. Since the label is \(y = 0\), the probability assigned to the labeled class is

\[p_y = 1 - p.\]

Assume the model is confident the point belongs to class 1:

\[p = 0.95, \qquad p_y = 0.05.\]

All gradients below are taken with respect to the logit \(z_y\) of the labeled class, using \(\frac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_y} = p_y(1-p_y)\).

docs.title: Cross entropy (CE)
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} = -\log p_y.\]

With \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} = -\log(0.05) \approx 3.00.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial z_y} = p_y - 1 = -0.95.\]

The gradient is close to its maximum magnitude. The noisy point pulls the decision boundary toward its wrong label as hard as a genuine misfit would.

docs.title: Generalized cross entropy (GCE)
docs.text:
Zhang and Sabuncu (2018) define

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GCE}} = \frac{1 - p_y^{\,q}}{q}, \qquad q \in (0, 1].\]

As \(q \to 0\) this recovers CE, and at \(q = 1\) it equals MAE.

With \(q = 0.7\) and \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GCE}} = \frac{1 - 0.05^{0.7}}{0.7} \approx \frac{1 - 0.123}{0.7} \approx 1.25.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GCE}}}{\partial z_y} = -\,p_y^{\,q}\,(1 - p_y) = -0.123 \times 0.95 \approx -0.117.\]

The GCE gradient equals the CE gradient multiplied by \(p_y^{\,q}\). This factor is the mechanism that reduces the effect of the noisy point: the more strongly the model disagrees with a label, the smaller that label’s influence on training.

docs.title: Focal loss (FL)
docs.text:
Lin et al. (2017) define

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FL}} = -(1 - p_y)^{\gamma} \log p_y.\]

With \(\gamma = 2\) and \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FL}} = (0.95)^2 \times 3.00 \approx 2.71.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FL}}}{\partial z_y} = (1 - p_y)^{\gamma}\bigl(\gamma\, p_y \log p_y + p_y - 1\bigr) \approx 0.9025 \times (-1.25) \approx -1.13.\]

The gradient is about \(1.2\times\) the CE gradient, not smaller. The modulating factor \((1 - p_y)^{\gamma} \approx 1\) when \(p_y\) is small, so focal loss leaves confidently wrong points essentially untouched.

Focal loss down-weights easy, correctly classified points (large \(p_y\)). That is useful for class imbalance, but it does nothing to suppress confidently wrong labels.

docs.title: Mean absolute error (MAE)
docs.text:
MAE is GCE with \(q = 1\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MAE}} = 1 - p_y.\]

With \(p_y = 0.05\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MAE}} = 0.95.\]

Gradient with respect to the logit:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MAE}}}{\partial z_y} = -\,p_y(1 - p_y) = -0.05 \times 0.95 \approx -0.05.\]

MAE gives the smallest push from the noisy point, but it learns slowly and can underfit.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Loss Value Logit gradient Relative to CE CE 3.00 \(-0.95\) \(1\times\) Focal (\(\gamma = 2\)) 2.71 \(-1.13\) \(\approx 1.2\times\) GCE (\(q = 0.7\)) 1.25 \(-0.12\) \(\approx 0.12\times\) MAE (\(q = 1\)) 0.95 \(-0.05\) \(\approx 0.05\times\)

docs.title: How GCE reduces the effect compared to CE
docs.text:
The gradient of CE with respect to the logit is \(p_y - 1\), which does not depend on how confident the model is that the label is wrong. GCE multiplies this gradient by \(p_y^{\,q}\):

  • Confident and correct points (\(p_y \approx 0.9\)): the factor is \(0.9^{0.7} \approx 0.93\), so training is nearly unchanged from CE.

  • Confident and wrong points (\(p_y \approx 0.05\), the noisy point): the factor is \(0.05^{0.7} \approx 0.12\), so the gradient shrinks by about \(8\times\).

The noisy point still contributes a small push, but the correctly labeled \(y=1\) cluster now dominates the boundary.

docs.title: Why focal loss does not help here
docs.text:
Focal loss scales the gradient by \((1 - p_y)^{\gamma}\), which is small when the model agrees with the label. GCE scales by \(p_y^{\,q}\), which is small when the model disagrees with the label. Those are opposite cases:

  • Focal loss reduces the weight of easy examples. It helps class imbalance but not label noise.

  • GCE reduces the weight of confidently disagreeing examples. It helps label noise but can underfit hard, correctly labeled minority examples.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• GCE cannot distinguish a noisy label from a hard but correct point. Both disagree with the model, so both are down-weighted.

  • A single point has a small effect. Many noisy points clustered together can still move the boundary, although each contributes less than under CE.

docs.title: Statistical Tests and \(p\)-Values
docs.text:
A \(p\)-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis \(H_0\) is true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

Every test in this section follows the same pipeline:

\[\text{data} \rightarrow \text{test statistic} \rightarrow \text{reference distribution under }H_0 \rightarrow \text{tail probability} \rightarrow p\text{-value}.\]

Only the statistic and the reference distribution change from test to test.

docs.title: One-Way Analysis of Variance
docs.text:
At a glance

One-way ANOVA compares variability between group means with variability within the groups:

\[\boxed{ F_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{ MS_{\mathrm{Between}} }{ MS_{\mathrm{Within}} }. }\]

The main formulas are

\[\boxed{ SS_{\mathrm{Between}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x})^2 }\] \[\boxed{ SS_{\mathrm{Within}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (x_{ij}-\bar{x}_i)^2 }\] \[\boxed{ df_{\mathrm{Between}}=k-1 }\] \[\boxed{ df_{\mathrm{Within}}=N-k }\]

and

\[\boxed{ p = P\left( F_{k-1,N-k} \geq F_{\mathrm{obs}} \right). }\]

The complete process is

\[\boxed{ \text{independent groups} \rightarrow \text{between- and within-group variation} \rightarrow F_{\mathrm{obs}} \rightarrow F\text{-distribution} \rightarrow p\text{-value}. }\]

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
One-way analysis of variance, commonly called one-way ANOVA, tests whether the population means of three or more independent groups are equal.

For example, suppose four methods are evaluated using results from independent experimental units:

\[\text{Method A},\quad \text{Method B},\quad \text{Method C},\quad \text{Method D}.\]

ANOVA tests whether the differences among the observed group means are larger than would reasonably be expected from random variation within the groups.

Although ANOVA is commonly used for three or more groups, it can also be used for two independent groups. With two groups, one-way ANOVA is equivalent to the equal-variance independent two-sample \(t\)-test:

\[F=t^2.\]

docs.title: When One-Way ANOVA Is Appropriate
docs.text:
One-way ANOVA is appropriate when:

  • there is one categorical explanatory variable;

  • the categorical variable contains two or more independent groups;

  • the outcome variable is numerical;

  • the objective is to compare the population means of the groups.

For example, the categorical variable may be the learning method:

\[\text{Method}\in\{A,B,C,D\},\]

and the numerical outcome may be AUCPR.

The word “one-way” means that the analysis contains one grouping factor.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Suppose there are \(k\) independent groups.

Let

\[x_{ij}\]

denote observation \(j\) from group \(i\), where

\[i=1,2,\ldots,k\]

and

\[j=1,2,\ldots,n_i.\]

Here:

  • \(k\) is the number of groups;

  • \(n_i\) is the number of observations in group \(i\);

  • \(N\) is the total number of observations.

The total sample size is

\[N=\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i.\]

The sample mean of group \(i\) is

\[\bar{x}_i = \frac{1}{n_i} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i}x_{ij}.\]

The grand mean across all observations is

\[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i}x_{ij}.\]

Equivalently, the grand mean is the weighted average of the group means:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i\bar{x}_i }{ N }.\]

docs.title: Hypotheses
docs.text:
The null hypothesis is that all population means are equal:

\[\boxed{ H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k. }\]

The alternative hypothesis is:

\[\boxed{ H_1: \text{not all population means are equal}. }\]

The alternative does not mean that every pair of population means is different. It means that at least one population mean differs from at least one other population mean.

For example, with three groups, the alternative may be true if

\[\mu_1=\mu_2\]

but

\[\mu_3\neq\mu_1.\]

docs.title: Basic Idea
docs.text:
ANOVA separates the total variability in the observations into two components:

\[\boxed{ \text{total variability} = \text{between-group variability} + \text{within-group variability}. }\]

Between-group variability measures how far the group means are from the grand mean.

Within-group variability measures how far individual observations are from their own group mean.

If \(H_0\) is true, both quantities estimate the same underlying population variance.

If the population means differ, the between-group variability tends to be large relative to the within-group variability.

docs.title: Total Sum of Squares
docs.text:
The total sum of squares measures the total variability of all observations around the grand mean:

\[\boxed{ SS_{\mathrm{Total}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (x_{ij}-\bar{x})^2. }\]

docs.title: Between-Group Sum of Squares
docs.text:
The between-group sum of squares measures the variability of the group means around the grand mean:

\[\boxed{ SS_{\mathrm{Between}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x})^2. }\]

Each squared difference is multiplied by \(n_i\) because a group mean represents \(n_i\) observations.

If all group means are close to the grand mean, then

\[SS_{\mathrm{Between}}\]

will be small.

If the group means are far apart, then

\[SS_{\mathrm{Between}}\]

will be large.

docs.title: Within-Group Sum of Squares
docs.text:
The within-group sum of squares measures the variability of observations around their respective group means:

\[\boxed{ SS_{\mathrm{Within}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (x_{ij}-\bar{x}_i)^2. }\]

This represents the variation that remains within groups after accounting for their different means.

It is also called the error sum of squares or residual sum of squares:

\[SS_{\mathrm{Error}}=SS_{\mathrm{Within}}.\]

docs.title: Decomposition of Variability
docs.text:
The total sum of squares can be decomposed as

\[\boxed{ SS_{\mathrm{Total}} = SS_{\mathrm{Between}} + SS_{\mathrm{Within}}. }\]

To understand this decomposition, write

\[x_{ij}-\bar{x} = (x_{ij}-\bar{x}_i) + (\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}).\]

The total deviation of an observation from the grand mean is the sum of:

  1. its deviation from its group mean;

  2. its group mean’s deviation from the grand mean.

Squaring and summing over all observations produces the ANOVA decomposition.

docs.title: Degrees of Freedom
docs.text:
The total degrees of freedom are

\[\boxed{ df_{\mathrm{Total}}=N-1. }\]

The between-group degrees of freedom are

\[\boxed{ df_{\mathrm{Between}}=k-1. }\]

The within-group degrees of freedom are

\[\boxed{ df_{\mathrm{Within}}=N-k. }\]

These satisfy

\[df_{\mathrm{Total}} = df_{\mathrm{Between}} + df_{\mathrm{Within}}.\]

Indeed,

\[N-1=(k-1)+(N-k).\]

docs.title: Mean Squares
docs.text:
The sums of squares depend on the number of observations and groups. Therefore, each sum of squares is divided by its degrees of freedom.

The between-group mean square is

\[\boxed{ MS_{\mathrm{Between}} = \frac{ SS_{\mathrm{Between}} }{ k-1 }. }\]

The within-group mean square is

\[\boxed{ MS_{\mathrm{Within}} = \frac{ SS_{\mathrm{Within}} }{ N-k }. }\]

The within-group mean square estimates the common population variance under the equal-variance ANOVA model.

docs.title: The \(F\)-Statistic
docs.text:
The ANOVA test statistic is

\[\boxed{ F_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{ MS_{\mathrm{Between}} }{ MS_{\mathrm{Within}} }. }\]

More explicitly,

\[\boxed{ F_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{ SS_{\mathrm{Between}}/(k-1) }{ SS_{\mathrm{Within}}/(N-k) }. }\]

The \(F\)-statistic compares variability between the group means with variability within the groups.

If \(H_0\) is true, both mean squares estimate the same population variance, so their ratio should generally be near one:

\[F_{\mathrm{obs}}\approx1.\]

If the group means differ substantially, the between-group mean square becomes large relative to the within-group mean square:

\[F_{\mathrm{obs}}>1.\]

A sufficiently large \(F\)-value provides evidence against \(H_0\).

docs.title: Theoretical \(F\)-Distribution
docs.text:
Under the null hypothesis, the ANOVA statistic follows an \(F\)-distribution:

\[F\sim F_{ u_1, u_2},\]

where

\[ u_1=k-1\]

is the numerator degrees of freedom and

\[ u_2=N-k\]

is the denominator degrees of freedom.

The probability density function of an \(F\)-distribution is

\[f(x; u_1, u_2) = rac{ 1 }{ B\left( rac{ u_1}{2}, rac{ u_2}{2} ight) } \left( rac{ u_1}{ u_2} ight)^{ u_1/2} x^{ u_1/2-1} \left( 1+ rac{ u_1}{ u_2}x ight)^{-( u_1+ u_2)/2}, \qquad x>0.\]

Here:

  • \(x\) is a possible value of the \(F\)-statistic;

  • \( u_1\) is the numerator degrees of freedom;

  • \( u_2\) is the denominator degrees of freedom;

  • \(B(\cdot,\cdot)\) is the beta function.

The beta function is related to the gamma function by

\[B(a,b) = rac{ \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) }{ \Gamma(a+b) }.\]

The \(F\)-distribution contains only nonnegative values and is generally right-skewed.

docs.title: Computing the \(p\)-Value
docs.text:
Large values of the \(F\)-statistic provide evidence against the null hypothesis. Therefore, ANOVA uses the right tail of the \(F\)-distribution:

\[ oxed{ p = P\left( F_{ u_1, u_2} \geq F_{\mathrm{obs}} \mid H_0 ight). }\]

If \(G_{ u_1, u_2}\) denotes the cumulative distribution function of the \(F\)-distribution, then

\[ oxed{ p = 1- G_{ u_1, u_2} (F_{\mathrm{obs}}). }\]

The standard ANOVA test does not use separate left-sided, right-sided, or two-sided alternatives. Deviations among group means in any direction increase the between-group sum of squares and therefore increase the \(F\)-statistic.

docs.title: Numerical Example
docs.text:
Suppose three independent methods produce the following scores:

\[\text{Method A}: 8,\;9,\;7,\] \[\text{Method B}: 5,\;6,\;4,\] \[\text{Method C}: 7,\;8,\;6.\]

There are

\[k=3\]

groups and

\[N=9\]

observations.

The group means are

\[\bar{x}_1=\frac{8+9+7}{3}=8,\] \[\bar{x}_2=\frac{5+6+4}{3}=5,\]

and

\[\bar{x}_3=\frac{7+8+6}{3}=7.\]

The grand mean is

\[\bar{x} = \frac{ 8+9+7+5+6+4+7+8+6 }{ 9 } = \frac{60}{9} = \frac{20}{3}.\]

The between-group sum of squares is

\[\begin{aligned} SS_{\mathrm{Between}} ={}& 3\left(8-\frac{20}{3}\right)^2 + 3\left(5-\frac{20}{3}\right)^2\\ &+ 3\left(7-\frac{20}{3}\right)^2. \end{aligned}\]

Therefore,

\[SS_{\mathrm{Between}}=14.\]

The within-group sum of squares is

\[\begin{aligned} SS_{\mathrm{Within}} ={}& \left[(8-8)^2+(9-8)^2+(7-8)^2\right]\\ &+ \left[(5-5)^2+(6-5)^2+(4-5)^2\right]\\ &+ \left[(7-7)^2+(8-7)^2+(6-7)^2\right]. \end{aligned}\]

Thus,

\[SS_{\mathrm{Within}}=6.\]

The degrees of freedom are

\[df_{\mathrm{Between}}=k-1=2,\]

and

\[df_{\mathrm{Within}}=N-k=6.\]

The mean squares are

\[MS_{\mathrm{Between}} = \frac{14}{2} = 7,\]

and

\[MS_{\mathrm{Within}} = \frac{6}{6} = 1.\]

Therefore, the observed \(F\)-statistic is

\[\boxed{ F_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{7}{1} = 7. }\]

Under \(H_0\),

\[F\sim F_{2,6}.\]

The \(p\)-value is

\[p=P(F_{2,6}\geq7).\]

A small right-tail probability provides evidence that not all three population means are equal.
